samples.hyp:
High dose pills can be tested on HIV patients with TB meningitis

A new trial will test a six-month treatment using high-dose anti-retroviral (ARV) treatment to prevent disability or death in people with HIV and multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and TB meningitis.

The trial, called THENDO, will look at the safety and efficacy of the high-dose anti-retroviral treatment in people with HIV and either MDR-TB or TB meningitis. It will look specifically at whether the treatment reduces the death rate and prevents or reduces central nervous system (CNS) related disability.

The trial is being conducted by the South African National TB Programme in collaboration with the University of Pretoria’s Research Unit in HIV Communications (R U H C), the University of KwaZulu-Natal, the University of Cape Town, the University of Johannesburg, the Durban Academic Hospital, the Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital, and the Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital.

The trial is being funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, which is supporting the trial through the Division of Acquired Immunodeficiency and Infectious Diseases.

The THENDO study will enrol 400 HIV-positive patients, aged 18 to 65 years, at 12 sites in South Africa. The participants will be randomly allocated to one of two groups: either standard care plus high-dose anti-retroviral treatment, or standard care alone.

However, many of these patients also develop meningitis, which is inflammation of the protective membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord. Standard doses of rifampicin can pass from the bloodstream into the brain, where they can be harmful. But Dr. Susan Mangwiro says there is a simple solution to this problem.

This solution is a drug that is already on the market and is not very expensive. The problem is that this drug is not prescribed to patients who need it.

Mangwiro is an assistant professor of neurology at the University of Zimbabwe. She is also the head of the country’s first neurocritical care unit.

She is currently researching the use of dexamethasone in treating HIV-related illnesses.

The drug has been used to treat other types of meningitis, but it has not been tested to see if it is effective against HIV-related illnesses.

Mangwiro and her colleagues decided to conduct a study to find out if the drug would be beneficial in treating these illnesses.

They recruited 55 HIV patients with meningitis and divided them into two groups.

One group received the usual treatment for this disease, which includes antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs.

The other group also received dexamethasone, which is a steroid that has anti-inflammatory properties.

The patients were then monitored to see if their symptoms improved after taking the drug.

The results of the study showed that the patients who received dexamethasone recovered faster than those who did not receive the drug.

They also had fewer side effects, such as nausea and vomiting.

Mangwiro says that dexamethasone is a cost-effective way to treat HIV-related illnesses, especially in developing countries where the number of HIV patients is high.

She adds that this drug could potentially save thousands of lives every year.

Mangwiro is optimistic that her research will encourage doctors in Zimbabwe and other African countries to prescribe dexamethasone to their HIV patients who also have meningitis.

She says this simple solution could greatly reduce the number of deaths from this disease.

Mangwiro’s research is a prime example of how simple solutions can have a profound impact on people’s lives.

It is also a reminder that sometimes, the key to solving a problem is something that is right in front of us.

All we need is the willingness to look and the open-mindedness to try new things.

Drugs in this class are given to many people with HIV because they can reduce the risk of transmitting the virus to an HIV-negative partner by more than 90%.


Professor Sarah Fidler, from the Department of Infectious Disease at the University of Birmingham, said: "These findings are important as they extend our understanding of how best to treat tuberculosis in people with HIV. We need well conducted trials to assess the best way forward.

"It is very unlikely that these findings will change current practice in the UK. Our results do, however, have important implications for other resource-constrained settings where the rifabutin-rifampicin switch is commonly used, and where the cost of an alternative therapy may be prohibitive."

Rifabutin is processed in the body in a way that makes it more soluble in the liquid that surrounds the brain, spine and skull. This means that it can get into these tissues more easily and does a better job of killing bacteria there. The study shows that the opposite is true for rifampicin.

"We need to better optimise the use of these drugs in people who need them the most, so this work is an important step towards improving the treatment of tuberculosis in people with HIV."

The researchers also wanted to find out if they could use the results to predict which patients would be best able to take the drug as capsules and which would be better served by intravenous doses.

The researchers enrolled 29 HIV-positive patients at a hospital in Johannesburg who had developed TB and were in the early stages of treatment. All of the patients received the standard initial dose of isoniazid and pyrazinamide for two weeks, and then were divided into three groups.

The first group received the standard dose of 600 mg of rifampicin once daily for two weeks. The second group received 600 mg of the drug as a capsule once daily, and the third group received their rifampicin at 600 mg daily but it was given to them intravenously.

The researchers then tested each patient’s blood to find out how much rifampicin their bodies had taken up based on the type of dose they received. They also measured the genetic activity of the rifampicin gene in each patient’s blood to see if the dose, no matter how it was given, had activated this gene, which would indicate the minimum dose needed to fight the TB infection.

After 8 weeks of treatment, all of the patients who received intravenous doses of rifampicin had levels of the drug in their blood 10 times higher than those who took the drug as a capsule. The group that took a standard oral dose had levels of the drug in their blood 1.5 times higher than the oral capsule group.

The minimum dose of the gene needed to fight the TB infection was found to be roughly 1 microgram/ml. Only one patient in the study had levels this high after taking a capsule, and 7 of the patients who received the intravenous version had these levels.

“We showed for the first time that the dose response of [rifampicin] can be predicted using the drug concentration at the indinudal level and the drug-induced change in transcription,” the authors wrote.

“Although our study was small, our data suggest that the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters that we have presented can be used as a guide for individualizing [rifampicin] therapy for patients with HIV and multidrug-resistant TB.”

This is a common problem in the field of psychology. Many people simply don’t want to participate in research, especially if it means being interrupted while they do everyday tasks. 

To try and overcome this issue, researchers are increasingly turning to methods that allow them to collect data without directly asking people for their participation. 

One such method is called “reaction time” or “key-press task” and has been used in many mobile phone studies. This involves showing people images or videos, and measuring the time it takes them to tap a button or press a key. 

This data is then compared to a known factor—like age or gender—to work out more information about how people behave in certain situations. 

For instance, a study from 2017 looked at how people react to images of snakes and spiders. 

This was done by showing 36 participants a series of images, including 18 of each type of creature. 

The participants were asked to tap a button as soon as they saw an image appear on the screen. 

From this, the researchers were able to work out how fast each person reacted to the images. 

They found that people took longer to react to snake images than spider images. 

This suggests that people find snake images more disturbing than spider images, even though the same number of each type of image was shown. 

This type of study is useful because it allows psychologists to collect data without directly asking people to take part. 

However, it’s important to note that this method isn’t without its drawbacks. 

For instance, it’s possible that people could have tapped the button accidentally, which would affect the results. 

Additionally, it’s unclear whether this method can be used to measure emotions or other internal states. 

Despite these limitations, many psychologists are interested in using this method in their research. 

For instance, a team of researchers in the UK is currently using this method to study how people respond to images of different objects. 

The aim of the study is to create a database of how people react to certain images, which can then be used to develop new treatments for mental health conditions.

To strengthen fertilizer use as a key instrument to increase food security, it is essential to understand why farmers do not always respond to economic incentives to adopt fertilizer. We developed an agent-based model of fertilizer decision-making to explore how the biophysical, socioeconomic, and policy-related factors interact and affect fertilizer use. The model incorporates fertilizer price, crop price, yield, and fertility as well as social learning and bio-physical feedbacks. We calibrated the model using data from smallholder farmers in Western Kenya and used the model to conduct a policy experiment, simulating the effect of different scenarios on fertilizer adoption. The model results show that fertilizer adoption is a complex function of multiple factors, and that no single intervention is likely to effectively change farmers' behavior. Our results suggest that the adoption of fertilizer is not only a function of economic incentives and fertilizer price but also a function of the perception of yield uncertainty, risk-spillover effects, and fellow farmers' behavior. We find that a 10% increase in the price of fertilizer is not likely to change the adoption of fertilizer significantly. Instead, a 10% increase in the price of crop could increase adoption by 1 percentage point, if the additional income is used to purchase fertilizer. We therefore conclude that programs aimed at making fertilizer more affordable, for example through input-subsidies, are more effective if subsidies are linked to the purchase of inputs at planting time instead of at harvest time, when the crop and cash are sold for consumption.

However, the long-term effect of combined application of biochar and compost is still unknown. Therefore, a field study was conducted over a period of three growing seasons (2014–2017) to investigate the short- and long-term effects of biochar and compost applications on soil microbial properties, nutrient pool, and plant growth and nutrition. The experiment was carried out in a Calcaric Tchernozem at the research field of the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna, in Austria (48° 14′ 39.52″ N, 16° 20′ 50.40″ E, 260 m a.s.l.).

The results showed that the positive effect of compost application was reduced with increasing compost age, and that the positive effect of biochar application was reduced under continuous compost application. Interactions between biochar and compost applications were observed at the microbial and nutrient pool level, but not at the level of plant growth and nutrition. Biochar enhanced the pool of microbial biomass after three compost applications per growing season, but not continuously. Compost application resulted in higher available phosphorus (HCl-extract) and potassium (acetate-lactate-extract) in the soil, but only at the beginning of the study. The highest total nutrient pool was found in soil that was treated with compost and biochar in each growing season. Soil microbial biomass and respiration as well as mineralizable nitrogen showed the highest results after application of compost and biochar in each growing season, but not continuously. Biochar has been shown to improve plant growth through changes in the chemical and physical properties of soils. However, little is known about the response of soil microbes to biochar. Soil microbes are crucial for soil health and biochar’s effects on plant growth could be partially mediated through changes in the soil microbial community. In this study, a range of laboratory-based biochar amendment experiments were conducted to determine the effects of biochar on the diversity and activity of soil microbes. In particular, changes in the abundance and activity of microbes that can promote plant growth (plant growth-promoting microbes) were investigated. Biochar, from cashew nut shell and cashew fruit waste, was produced from laboratory-scale slow pyrolysis processes. Soils were collected from sites in Uganda and Kenya and brought to the laboratory. Biochar amendment experiments were conducted in the laboratory using the collected soils. The biochar amendment levels were either 1% or 2% by weight. Control treatments without biochar were also included. Soil microbial response was assessed using a range of methods. These included: measuring changes in soil respiration; transforming biochar into a form that allows for the quantification of microbial biomass; measuring changes in the abundance of a group of microbes that produce antibiotics known to protect plants from disease; and measuring changes in the overall diversity of soil microbes. Results from this study showed that the production of biochar from cashew waste does not significantly alter the diversity of soil microbes. Furthermore, biochar did not significantly alter the amount of soil respiration, microbial biomass, or overall microbial diversity. However, the biochar used in this study did increase the abundance of bacteria that produce antibiotics to control plant pathogens. These results suggest that biochar application in sub-Saharan Africaan farms may not significantly affect the diversity of soil microbial communities or soil microbial activity. However, biochar does have the potential to reduce plant disease by increasing the abundance of beneficial bacteria in soil.

The experiment was set up in a randomized block design with fifteen treatments and three replicates. The treatments were: control, 5 and 10 t ha−1 biochar, 2.5 and 5 t ha−1 compost alone, increasing rates of biochar with compost (5 t ha−1 compost + 2.5 t ha−1 biochar, 5 t ha−1 compost + 5 t ha−1 biochar), and inverse treatments (5 t ha−1 biochar + 2.5 t ha−1 compost, 5 t ha−1 biochar + 5 t ha−1 compost). The results showed that biochar had a positive effect on soil respiration after 1.5 months. Compost and biochar applied together or alternately improved soil pH more than the individual treatments. The amount of carbon was not significantly affected by the treatments, but compost and biochar added together or alternately increased the amount of nitrogen in the soil. Biochar had a positive effect on soil respiration and the interaction of biochar and compost had a positive synergistic effect on the amount of total microbes and the C:N ratio. The application of biochar alone or together with compost improved the quality of soil.

The biochars had high concentrations of C, and the surface functional groups increased as the pyrolysis temperature increased, but the surface area and pore volume (at diameters less than 5 nm) decreased with increasing pyrolysis temperature. The coconut biochar had the largest particle size distribution in the 0.05–2.00 mm size range, while the rice husk biochar had the smallest.

Application of biochars to soil at the greater rate increased soil EC, pH, and C content, and decreased soil saturation water content and bulk density. The opposite effect was observed for the anions SO42− and HPO42−, with a decrease in sorption capacity with increasing biochar application rate.

This means that compost or biochar addition to soil increased microbial respiration.

Biochar is a type of charcoal that is created when organic matter is heated in the absence of oxygen. It has been shown to improve soil structure, increase water holding capacity and supply plant nutrients, and has characteristics that make it durable in the environment.

The study also found that the addition of compost at 20 metric tons per hectare with either biochar or rice husk biochar resulted in the largest increase in basal respiration. The combination of compost with biochar is of particular interest because the biochar in this combination may help bind soil nutrients, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and prevent their leaching.

The study was conducted in an upland rice field in Luzon, the Philippines. The researchers established 24 experimental plots, each with a single rice plant, and added either compost alone, rice husk biochar alone, corn cob biochar alone, or a combination of compost and biochar. The researchers found that while basal respiration rates increased with the addition of either biochar or compost, the combination of compost and biochar resulted in the highest increase.

The researchers also found that the combination of compost with either type of biochar resulted in more water being stored in the soil. This means that the combination of compost and biochar may help plants access the water they need during dry periods.

These results are really interesting, as they indicate that the effect of biochar on soil is dependent on the source material used to produce it. This means that in order to maximize the positive effects of biochar on soil quality and crop yield, careful selection of the feedstock used to make biochar is key.

It is also important to note that the effects of biochar on soil quality can vary depending on the measurement used to assess them. In our study, the effects of biochar on soil were measured using the following three proxies: soil microbial biomass, a surrogate for soil microbial community function; soil respiration, a surrogate for soil microbial community size; and enzyme activity, a measure of the capacity for soil microbes to hydrolyze organic compounds. All three proxies provided different insights into the effects of biochar on soil quality.

The choice of measurement is important because it reflects different properties of the soil microbial community. For example, soil respiration measures the energy status of the soil microbial community as a whole, while soil microbial biomass gives insight into small and medium-sized members of the soil microbial community. Large members of the soil microbial community, like fungi, are difficult to account for because they do not fit into the size category of the methods used to measure soil microbial biomass. However, their role in the soil microbial community cannot be overlooked, especially when it comes to plant disease suppression and the solanization of soil (1). Therefore, it is important to use multiple proxies to get a comprehensive understanding of how management practices, like the use of biochar, affect the soil microbial community.

The results of this study show that the effects of biochar on the soil microbial community can be accurately measured, and that different measurements can provide different information regarding the nature and scope of those effects. This is important for two reasons. First, it implies that effects of biochar on the soil microbial community can also be measured in other soils around the world, as the measured responses were within the range of what has been previously reported in other studies (2). Second, it shows that in order to get a comprehensive understanding of the impacts of biochar on the soil microbial community, multiple measurements need to be made, using multiple methods that provide information on different properties of the soil microbial community.

The ICRD was organized by the World Federation of Rheumatology (WFR), the Kuwait Rheumatology Association (KuRA) and the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research (KISR). The meeting brought together experts from around the world to discuss the most up-to-date issues in the field of rheumatic diseases. The meeting was attended by 367 delegates from 41 countries. The congress was held at the Four Seasons Hotel, Kuwait.

The following is an abstract of the presentation made by Dr. Rizwan Sarwar on “The Atypical Fibrin Fibre Network in Rheumatoid Arthritis and its Relation to Autoimmunity, Inflammation and Thrombosis”:

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is the most common systemic autoimmune disease, affecting ~1% of the population worldwide.

A fundamental defect in RA is the deposition of immune-complexes and altered fibrin(ogen) in the form of intracellular and/or extracellular fibers and networks.

These fibers and networks have an atypical topography, biochemistry and function compared to fibrin formed during the coagulation cascade.

The role of fibrin in RA goes way beyond the traditional concept of a simple structural protein involved in wound healing and hemostasis.

Our recent findings using 3D-SDS are that RA fibrin is more oligomeric, has a higher ratio of fibrinogen alpha to gamma chains, and is more readily cleaved by the endogenous proteinase, tissue plasminogen activator, than non-RA fibrin.

These findings suggest that the current coagulation model underestimates the body’s response to immune-complex deposition.

RA fibrin may therefore be viewed as a danger signal that when recognized by the innate immune system triggers the deposition of immune-complexes and autoantibodies, chronic inflammation, and the damage of bone and cartilage.

RA fibrin associated thrombosis may represent a distinct entity, distinct from other fibrin associated thromboses, requiring novel approaches to prevention and treatment.

This is just one of the many thought-provoking presentations made during the three days of the congress. In active RA, the levels of fibrinogen, D-dimer, and C-reactive protein (CRP) are higher than in patients with other inflammatory conditions and healthy controls. However, the levels of antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S are higher in patients with RA than in patients with other rheumatic diseases and healthy controls. These findings are consistent with a procoagulant (fibrinolytic) state in RA. The underlying mechanism for this apparent paradox is not known. However,, the levels of tissue factor (TF) and soluble TF are increased in RA, which may explain the coagulation findings in RA. The increased levels of soluble TF in RA could explain the decreased protein C levels and increased D-dimer levels via the extrinsic pathway. Furthermore, the increased levels of tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) could also explain the increased protein C levels via the same pathway. The increased levels of TF in RA could be due to increased expression of TF by synovial tissue and/or increased degradation of TF by metalloproteinases.

We have previously shown that the anticitrulline antibody, which is present at high levels in RA patients, binds to citrullinated fibrin and that this binding is associated with accelerated fibrinolysis during clot lysis in patients. The aim of this study was to further elucidate the interaction between antibodies to citrullinated fibrin and fibrin structure. Methods. Nineteen clots were obtained from 10 RA patients. The degree of citrullination was analyzed with the RA antibody HIG1. Antibodies to citrullinated fibrin were analyzed with ELISA using fibrin monomers, HIG1, and clots as antigens. The fibrin structure was studied by electron microscopy. Results. All patients had antibodies to citrullinated fibrin. The OD values of the ELISA for the different antigens varied considerably between patients, for fibrin monomers (0.15–0.60), HIG1 (0.01–1.00), and clots (0.10–0.95). The antibodies recognized different epitopes on the fibrin monomer as well as on the clots. The antibodies bound to different parts of the fibrin structure as seen by electron microscopy. Conclusion. Antibodies to citrullinated fibrin recognize several different epitopes on the fibrin molecule. This indicates a rather unspecific interaction. However, since the antibodies bind to different parts of the fibrin structure, the interaction may influence the fibrin structure.

Published: 09/12/2019 11:45 PM

Source: University of Rochester Medical Center

Blood clotting in arthritis patients may explain their increased risk for heart attack, stroke

Credit: University of Rochester Medical Center

A new study led by a University of Rochester Medical Center physician has found that people living with rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to have a genetic variant that causes blood to clot, which could explain their increased risk of heart attack and stroke.

The study, published online in the journal Arthritis & Rheumatology, is the first to link this specific genetic variation to both cardiovascular disease and rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic autoimmune disease that causes pain, swelling, and stiffness in the joints. While the exact cause of rheumatoid arthritis is not known, previous research has shown that inflammation and blood clotting play a role in the development of the disease.

“We’ve known for a while that people with rheumatoid arthritis have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, especially within the first six months of diagnosis,” said first author Victoria Guan, M.D., Ph.D., a rheumatologist at URMC and a researcher in the Center for Translational Neuromuscular Research. “We also know that inflammatory arthritis patients need to be treated like people at high risk for heart attack or stroke. But the mechanisms underlying this increased risk are not clear. Our data suggests that a clotting disorder, in part, may be to blame.”

Using electronic health records and a custom-designed algorithm, Guan and her colleagues created a genetic match between 823 people with rheumatoid arthritis and 1,421 people without the disease to look for differences in variants of a gene that is linked to blood clotting. This gene, called Factor V, has previously been shown to play a role in both cardiovascular disease and autoimmune thyroid disease. The researchers, whose work was funded by the National Institutes of Health, the Arthritis National Research Foundation, and the Rochester Clinical & Translational Science Center, found that 16 percent of the rheumatoid arthritis group carried a rare variant of the Factor V gene, compared to just six percent of those without the disease.

Further supporting the link between the gene variant and blood clotting was a look at the medical records of the study’s participants. The researchers found that those with the Factor V variant were more likely to have had a blood clot, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism, and were more likely to have received blood thinners.

The study was conducted by a team of researchers from the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine and Massachusetts General Hospital and Boston Children’s Hospital and it was published in Science Translational Medicine.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune condition that causes inflammation in the lining of the joints, leading to pain, stiffness, and swelling in the hands, feet, and other body parts. It can also affect other organs in the body, such as the heart and lungs. In addition to physical symptoms, rheumatoid arthritis can have a significant impact on mental health, leading to depression and anxiety.

The researchers were interested in understanding the link between rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular disease. Previous studies have suggested that individuals with rheumatoid arthritis have a higher risk of developing cardiovascular conditions, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood.

The team used a mouse model to simulate human rheumatoid arthritis. They induced the condition by injecting mice with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which is a component of the cell wall of certain bacteria. The mice developed inflammation in their joints, similar to human rheumatoid arthritis.

They then conducted a series of experiments to investigate the effects of rheumatoid arthritis on the cardiovascular system. They found that the mice with rheumatoid arthritis developed changes in their blood vessels, including inflammation and thickening of the vessel walls. This can interfere with proper blood flow and increase the risk of blood clots.

The researchers also found that the mice with rheumatoid arthritis had changes in their immune system, which could potentially contribute to the increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Specifically, they found that a protein called interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta) was activated in the immune cells of the rheumatoid arthritis mice, and this activation was linked to the development of cardiovascular changes.

The researchers then conducted experiments to see if targeting IL-1beta could prevent the cardiovascular changes associated with rheumatoid arthritis. They used a drug called canakinumab, which is a monoclonal antibody that blocks the activity of IL-1beta. When the rheumatoid arthritis mice were treated with canakinumab, the cardiovascular changes were prevented, and the mice’s blood vessels returned to normal.

In the current study, the researchers set out to see whether these blood changes were associated with markers of heart disease. 

They found that RA patients had higher levels of D-dimer – a marker of blood clotting activity – and several markers of heart damage, including N-terminal prohormone B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitivity Troponin I (hsTnI), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP).

“Future studies should focus on the clinical significance of this marker in RA patients, in order to develop strategies for the early detection of CVD in this high-risk population,” they write. 

“Early diagnosis of CVD in RA could lead to better outcomes for patients and improve their quality of life,” they conclude.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are known to be at greater risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) — the leading cause of disability, hospitalization, and death in RA patients. However, the exact relationship between the two diseases is unclear. Previous studies investigating the association between RA and CVD have produced inconsistent results, leading some researchers to conclude that RA is not associated with an increased risk of CVD, while others note a clear link between the two disorders.

Abstract:  National oceanographic agencies have a mandate to provide accurate forecasts of marine weather conditions to ocean users. In the United States, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) supports a number of regional meteorological centers that produce marine forecasts. The forecasts produced are of high quality, yet ocean users have not consistently indicated a high level of satisfaction. A survey of Maine lobstermen reveals that weather forecasts from shore-based sources are considered very useful, although respondents indicated that they do not check forecasts frequently and do not change their fishing decisions as a result of the forecasts. The importance of understanding the perceptions of users and the impact of the forecasts on user decisions is recognized, and the paper discusses the importance of marine meteorological forecasts and the impact they have on user decisions. The paper describes a survey designed to probe users' perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors regarding marine forecasts. The survey includes questions on respondents' demographics, their marine weather forecasting behaviors, their perceptions of the accuracy and utility of the forecasts, and the impacts of the forecasts on their fishing decisions. The survey is currently being replicated in other New England states. The results of the survey will be used to improve the message being delivered to ocean users and to identify ways to better focus marine forecasts on the information needs of the users.

The usability gap refers to the difference between the amount of scientific information that is needed by the public to make decisions about policy and the amount of scientific information that the public actually wants to know. The usability gap has been identified as a barrier to effective science communication. To address this barrier, we aim to better understand the public’s information needs and preferences in the context of scientific research related to genetically modified crops (GMCs). Public attitudes towards GMCs have been widely studied, but there is less research examining the public’s preferences for information about GMCs and scientists’ communication practices. A survey of scientific literature shows that public attitudes towards GMCs can vary depending on how the technology is framed and that scientists typically overestimate the negative public reactions to GMCs. Additionally, there is a general discrepancy between scientists’ perceptions of the public’s interest in scientific discussions about GMCs and the public’s actual interest in these discussions. We designed our survey to address these discrepancies by (1) examining how the public wants to receive information about GMCs and (2) testing the effectiveness of different modes of information delivery. We administered our survey in the form of an online questionnaire to 500 U.S. adults and received 370 responses. Our results show that the public is interested in receiving information about GMCs and would like to receive this information from multiple sources. Additionally, we found that combining different modes of information delivery, such as videos and interactive infographics, can be an effective way to reach and engage a broad audience. Our results also show that the public has a high level of trust in scientific institutions, which can be useful for effective communication about controversial topics, such as GMCs. Overall, our findings suggest that science communication efforts can be improved by aligning scientists’ information supply with the public’s information demand. In the context of GMCs, this can be done by increasing the quantity and quality of scientific information that the public finds interesting and useful and by employing communication strategies that leverage the public’s preferences for information delivery. By closing the usability gap, scientists can help the public make evidence-based decisions about GMCs and ensure that scientific research can inform public policy in a meaningful way.

To address these questions, a total of 1,500 people completed online surveys, and 160 individuals participated in semi-structured interviews as part of a larger study led by Dr. Jennifer D. Taras, Associate Professor at the University of Guelph.

Dr. Taras and colleagues used a mixed methods approach to explore the perceptions of stakeholders from across Canada. They found that the greatest interest in seasonal forecasting was to support adaptation and decision-making for agriculture, with interest waning for hydrological, weather, and climate forecasts. This was consistent with participants’ perceptions of the potential benefits and greater usability of forecasting information for agriculture (due, in part, to its routine and predictable application). In general, respondents were more interested in near-term forecasts, with decreasing interest as the forecast horizon lengthened – this was observed for all forecast types. In addition to this, for hydrological forecasts, the most highly ranked benefit was to improve flood preparedness, while for weather and climate forecasts, the most highly ranked benefit was to improve everyday activities.

“Stakeholders were most interested in how well a forecasting tool met their needs in supporting decision-making related to agriculture, and least interested in the accuracy of the tool or the underlying science,” says Dr. Taras. “For some individuals, accuracy was not seen as critical since forecast information would be used for preparatory purposes even in the absence of 100% certainty.”

Dr. Taras and colleagues also explored the factors that impact the perceived risks and benefits of seasonal forecasting, and potential risks and benefits of using forecast information. The most frequently cited benefit of seasonal forecasting was that it provided timely and/or forecasted information that improved planning and decision-making. The most frequently cited risk was that forecast information was not specific enough to be actionably useful. When ranking the importance of various factors that impact the risks and benefits of seasonal forecasting, stakeholders identified the usefulness of the forecast information (for the sector of interest) as the most important factor that increased the benefits, while the accuracy of the forecast and newness of the technology were considered the risk-increasing factors most in need of research.

“Overall, the results of this study suggest that it is important to carefully consider the risks and benefits from the user’s perspective and to communicate the relative importance of these risks and benefits when developing seasonal forecasting services and tools,” says Dr. Taras. “Forecast-based decision-making will be most effective when forecast information is relevant, easy to understand, and able to be quickly acted upon.”

South Africans and New Zealanders are more likely to trust weather forecasts about the weather at sea than about the weather on land, according to a new study from the University of Otago.

The study, co-authored by Otago geography professor Dr Tim Schwandt and Otago marketing lecturer Dr Carey van Marrewijk, is the first to compare the trust people place in forecasts for marine and terrestrial weather.

The researchers used data from a survey of 11 countries, including New Zealand and South Africa, and found that both South Africans and New Zealanders were among the most likely to trust marine weather forecasts.

The study used a survey from the International Social Survey Programme, which is based at the University of Michigan, USA.

Dr Schwandt says the study is important because trust in sources of weather information is important for public and policy debate about climate change.

“While there are good scientific reasons to believe that the climate is changing, there is still a lot of public uncertainty about the extent of climate change, and whether it is human-induced,” Dr Schwandt says.

“People’s beliefs about the extent of climate change are strongly related to how much they trust sources of climate information, which in turn affects their views about climate policies and their willingness to make sacrifices to address climate change.”

The study found that people are more likely to trust weather forecasts if they live in a country with a strong democratic culture, if they have a high level of education, and if they personally experience weather events.

“People who live in countries with strong democratic cultures may be more trusting because they are accustomed to evaluating information about important issues in their community,” Dr Schwandt says.

“Similarly, higher education may expose people to a broad range of perspectives on scientific and social questions, which could increase their trust in expert sources of information.

“Finally, personal experience of weather events may increase people’s trust in weather forecasts because it confirms the expertise of meteorologists, and because it gives people a sense that they understand how the weather works.”

samples.src: In this study researchers chose to look at how people in South Africa and New Zealand use forecasting services – both countries have long coastlines, but have vastly different populations and coastal conditions.
samples.ref: Mu kunoonyereza kuno abanoonyereza baasalawo okutunuulira engeri abantu mu South Afirika ne New Zealand gye bakozesaamu okuteebereza– amawanga gombi galina embalama empanvu, naye balina abantu ab’enjawulo n’embeera z’obudde ez’enjawulo ku mbalama.
samples.hyp:
In South Africa, where most of the population lives in cities, few people work in the fishing industry. In New Zealand, most people living in the coastal regions work in the fishing industry or a related field. In both countries, researchers used in-depth interviews with fishermen, fishery managers, and academics to gain an understanding of how they use forecasts. They also conducted systematic surveys of the fishers. In South Africa, they surveyed 76 fishers, and in New Zealand, they surveyed 89 fishers. The researchers found that in both countries, fishers’ most important use of forecasts was to plan their work activities, such as when to go fishing. In New Zealand, where most fishers work on their own boats, they also used forecasts to decide whether to hire extra hands or not. In South Africa, where most fishers work for someone else on a shared boat, they used forecasts to decide whether to start work early. In both countries, fishers relied on forecasts that were easy to understand and that gave specific and detailed information about wind speed and direction, sea temperature, and wave height. Most of the fishers in both countries also indicated that forecasts should be available in a format that they can access on their phones. This is an important consideration because it is usually the people working on the boats who need the forecasts the most, and cell phone use at sea is common. However, in New Zealand, where most fishers work year-round and have fixed channels for selling their fish, forecasts were not important for when they sold their fish. In South Africa, where most fishers take their fish to the market and can sell to whoever will pay the most, forecasts influence when they go fishing. If forecasts predict good conditions, then the fishers will try to go fishing early in the morning to get the most fish, and the most money, as the retail market opens. However, if the forecasts are predicting bad conditions, they may choose to not go fishing at all. This shows that forecasts can have different importance to people in different situations. It is important for forecast providers to understand the specific situations of the people receiving their forecasts, so that they can provide forecasts that are most useful.

(ABC News)

These are important factors in light of how future climate change might impact weather forecasting. (ABC News)

The study also found that climate change is causing more frequent and intense droughts in the southwestern U.S. The researchers found that the probability of megadroughts — 20-year droughts or longer — in the region had increased more than 5-fold since 2000.

“Megadrought conditions are ongoing in the Southwestern U.S. and show few signs of abating in the near future,” the study said.

The scientists noted that their study looked only at the role that climate change is playing in droughts in the region, and didn’t consider other factors such as water management decisions that might also be impacting drought conditions.

Still, the new findings should be a major concern for those who live in the region, said study co-author Park Williams.

“If you live in the Southwest and you have lived through a megadrought before, this means you and your community should be planning for the next one,” said Williams, who is with Columbia University’s Earth Institute.

The research “is a jolt to our collective conscience,” said climatologist Jonathan Overpeck, also with the University of Arizona.

Overpeck said he was stunned by how much worse the drought conditions could be by the end of the century. “This is not going to be good,” he said.

The new study, published online May 10 in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, was based on computer simulations of weather patterns using an average of data from 11 climate models.

To determine if climate change had played a role in the droughts, the researchers compared data from the simulations with data from a second set of computer simulations that didn’t include climate change.

The simulations found that climate change is responsible for an additional 35% to 50% of the megadrought risk in the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah, and an additional 15% to 40% in the Colorado River Basin.

Currently, the Southwest is in its 19th year of drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor, a collaboration between federal and academic agencies.

The last megadrought in the region, which occurred from 1899 to 1905, was the country’s longest and worst drought, study co-author Jonathan Overpeck has said previously.

Even though the current drought is not quite there yet, “we’re getting there,” Williams said.

samples.ref: Enkozesa y’enkola keetabya mu kukebera obutuukamu bw’enkola z’obulimi ez’enjawulo mu kubala obulungi embeera y’obudde:

A Case Study From Northern Benin

This chapter investigates the potential of participatory methods to assess the climate resilience of agricultural interventions. It presents a framework for participatory climate resilience assessment and applies this framework in a case study from northern Benin. The results show that the proposed approach can help to (1) reveal the diverse and dynamic strategies farmers use to cope with climate variability and change, (2) identify the scope for climate-smart interventions, and (3) prioritize adaptation options. The chapter discusses lessons learned in applying the proposed approach and reflects on its potential, limitations, and further applications.

Keywords: Climate change, Adaptation, Food security, Participatory approach, West Africa, CCAFS Program

The full text of this chapter is available in PDF format.

samples.hyp:
Study: A Descriptive Epidemiological Study of the Incidence of Tuberculosis among School Students in a Rural Area in Lushoto, Tanzania

Tuberculosis (TB) is a major public health problem in Tanzania, as it is in many other parts of the world. Each year, approximately 12,000 new cases of TB occur in Tanzania, and about one-quarter of these are among children [1; p. 3]. The proportion of children with TB relative to the adult cases is not known, but it is believed to be small because the child population is relatively small compared to the adult population, and because children are generally thought to be less susceptible to TB infection than are adults [2; p. 1–2]. Because of this, children are not usually considered when control strategies are developed, although it is believed that the role of children in the transmission of TB has been underestimated [2; p. 1–2].

The development of effective control strategies for TB depends on a clear understanding of the epidemiology of TB, including knowledge of the risk factors for the development of active disease following a prior infection with a latent form of the bacteria [3; p. 1]. The overall aim of this case study was to identify the incidence of TB among school students in a rural area in Lushoto, Tanzania, and to determine the risk factors for the development of active pulmonary TB among these students.

Methods

Study site and population

This case study was conducted in the rural area of Lushoto, which is located in the northern part of Tanzania, and is known for its high rate of TB [4; p. 2]. The study population consisted of all students in primary and secondary schools in the rural area of Lushoto. The student population was approximately 17,000, and included students from 69 primary schools, and 4 secondary schools. The area is characterized by a temperate climate with two distinct seasons: a rainy season from April to November, and a dry season from December to March. The average annual temperature is 18.7°C, and the annual rainfall is 1,340 mm [5; p. 2]. In 2004 there were approximately 60,000 people living in the rural area of Lushoto [6; p. 2].

The objectives of this study were to: (1) provide an overview of the current state of CSA research in Africa; (2) identify knowledge gaps and research needs to advance CSA in Africa; and (3) provide recommendations for future research and application of CSA in African contexts.

A keyword search of Web of Science, Scopus, and Agricola databases using ‘agriculture’ and ‘Africa’ as well as ‘agroecology’ and ‘Africa’ as search terms was conducted, and the bibliographic references of identified articles and book chapters were traced to identify additional relevant articles. The ‘Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) Inclusion Meter’ (CSAIM) was developed to assess the extent to which specific agricultural practices are aligned with the CSA principles of efficiency, balance, and adaptation. The framework of the CSAIM is based on the multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) approach and uses a normalized weighted scoring system to assign a CSA-compatibility score to a given agricultural practice. The score is calculated based on the principles of equally weighted and fully decomposable criteria. The method is participatory and requires the intervention to be assessed to be evaluated by a group of experts according to the importance and relevance of each criterion to the context of interest. The CSAIM protocol can be used to assess interventions at various stages of their implementation and can be used to evaluate the merit of different interventions in terms of their alignment to the CSA principles. The method also provides an opportunity for e.g. practitioners and stakeholders to actively engage in the assessment process and thus, promote a sense of ownership of the results. The method could potentially be applied to any agricultural intervention aimed at improving the efficiency and sustainability of agricultural practices.

The CSA principles were identified based on a systematic literature review and expert consultations. Three high-level principles were identified; namely, efficiency, balance, and adaptation. A total of 27 sub-criteria were identified under these principles (Fig. 1).

[... ... ...]

We developed a CSAIM protocol that consists of a scoring system and a method for applying the system to assess the CSA-compatibility of a given agricultural intervention. The method is multi-criteria in nature and can be applied to various types of interventions as well as at different stages of their implementation. The CSAIM uses a normalized scoring system that is based on equal weighting of criteria and fully decomposable criteria.

[... ... ...]

samples.src: New monitoring techniques help scientists and farmers prepare for climate change
samples.ref: Obukodyo bw’okulondoola obupya buyamba bannassaayansi n’abalimi okwetegekera enkyukakyuka y’embeera y’obudde
samples.hyp:
A new technique for monitoring the abundance and distribution of important soil organisms could help scientists and farmers prepare for climate change.

The technique, developed by researchers at the University of Georgia, allows scientists to assess the impact of climate change on soil organisms and provides farmers and land managers a new tool to evaluate the health of soil ecosystems.

The study, published online recently in the Soil Science Society of America Journal, reveals that soil fauna - such as springtails, Collembola; nematodes, roundworms; and enchytraeids, potworms - are good indicators of soil climate because the organisms are easily impacted by temperature and moisture.

Soil fauna provide ecosystem services, including the decomposition of organic matter, that support aboveground biodiversity and soil productivity. This makes the fauna particularly useful to farmers and land managers interested in preparing for climate change.

"We are just starting to understand how global climate change will impact organisms in the soil and useful methods for monitoring the effects," said Herbert Gleick, corresponding author of the study and a research scientist in the Department of Natural Resources and the Environment in the UGA College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences. "This is the first study to demonstrate that soil fauna can be used to detect changes in soil climate."

To determine if soil fauna could be used to monitor the effects of climate change, the researchers first established a baseline of fauna abundance and distribution at seven sites across Georgia. They then monitored soil fauna at four of the seven sites where recent climate data indicated changes in temperature and moisture.

The researchers found that the abundance and distribution of soil fauna varied across the state and that different groups of soil fauna were affected differently by climate change. Enchytraeids were most sensitive to changes in moisture, while nematodes were most sensitive to changes in temperature.

"Because climate change is predicted to increase in magnitude and frequency around the world, these results not only advance our understanding of how soil climate is changing in Georgia, but also provide a new and useful tool for monitoring the effects of climate change around the world," Gleick said.

This is thanks to a new study that developed a reliable method to measure how much carbon is stored in the soil.

Soil is one of the main ways that carbon is stored safely from the atmosphere. It removes carbon dioxide that would otherwise accumulate in the air and cause global warming. The challenge is to understand how much carbon is being stored in the soil, and this new study helps researchers take another step forward in answering this question.

Soil carbon is also important for healthy soil and productive farms. Soils with high carbon store more water, have higher yields and are more fertile. Measuring carbon in the soil helps smallholder farmers and scientists work together to develop practices that keep carbon in the soil, where it is safely stored.

In the new study, researchers worked with farmers in Tanzania to test how effective different practices are at keeping carbon in the soil. The practices included different combinations of planting crops, adding animal manure, or leaving certain areas of the soil unplanted.

The researchers were able to develop a new method that allows them to accurately measure how much carbon is in the soil. This method can be used by scientists and farmers in Tanzania and other African countries to help develop new ways to strengthen food security while keeping carbon out of the atmosphere.

samples.src: “Climate-smart agriculture” is something the United Nations encourages to help small-scale farmers prepare for climate change.
samples.ref: “Obulimi obutambulira ku kubala obulungi embeera y’obudde” ky’ekintu Amawanga Amagatte gye gakubiriza okukola okusobola okuyamba abalimi abalimira ku ttaka ettono okwetegekera enkyukakyuka y’embeera y’obudde.
samples.hyp:
The concept is a guide for agriculture policies and practices that aim to increase productivity, while also adapting and contributing to mitigation actions regarding climate change.

A new study says the approach has potential, but more research is needed to help it live up to its promise.

The study, published in Nature, is the first to evaluate the evidence base for climate-smart agriculture.

Lead author Anthony Baranzelli, a postdoctoral associate at Cornell University, said climate-smart agriculture is still a new idea and this is the first time the body of research behind it has been brought together.

“We found that there are some knowledge gaps, and in some cases, the evidence base is limited,” he said. “But overall, we found that climate-smart agriculture has a lot of potential.”

To evaluate the evidence base, the researchers developed 44 unique evidence pairs. An evidence pair consists of an individual study and a specific claim or claims derived from that study.

The researchers looked at 295 individual studies that involved 14 claim types. Each study was evaluated to determine the strength of evidence for each claim it supported.

The researchers also looked at how well the studies were designed to measure the impact of climate smart agriculture on the four pillars of climate-smart agriculture: increasing productivity, adapting to climate change, contributing to mitigation, and making agriculture more resilient.

The researchers found 30 of the claim types had a medium amount of evidence, four had a large amount of evidence and 10 had very little evidence. They also found that less than 10 percent of the studies evaluated looked at how climate smart agriculture affects resilience.

Baranzelli said the concept of climate-smart agriculture is still new and more research is needed. However, the study shows the approach has the potential to be effective.

“Future research should focus more on the adaptation and mitigation claims,” he said. “And we need to look more at how climate smart agriculture affects the four pillars of the approach.”

Photo: C. Kozar, CIAT

Climate change is one of the most serious and most likely threats to food security, particularly in countries south of the Sahara. Higher temperatures lower labor productivity, reduce the quality and quantity of food produced, and contribute to more extreme weather, such as intense droughts and heavy downpours.

The good news is that researchers are working on a number of solutions that can help farmers and food producers adapt to climate change, such as developing heat-tolerant crops, finding irrigation solutions to deal with drought, and encouraging farmers to practice conservation agriculture.

But these solutions are in the early stages and we need more research to find more ways to make farming more climate resilient. And the food systems that supply the world’s population with nourishment are also in need of a revamp. We need to make them more resilient, sustainable, inclusive, and diverse.

The CGIAR Research Program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CC-AFS) is a partnership of 15 international centers and the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF), working to strengthen agricultural systems to adapt to climate change. We have developed a research strategy that has five main goals:

  1. Increasing the resilience and sustainability of agricultural and food systems to climate change, while improving food security and reducing poverty
  2. Reducing the vulnerability of food production systems and communities to climate change through improved understanding and application of climate information
  3. Enhancing the capacity of citizens to adapt to climate change through transformation of social institutions
  4. Improving the quality of life of the poor through climate-smart agriculture
  5. Strengthening the ability of CGIAR and its partners to sustain and upscale impact from climate-related research and practice

The interventions were implemented by a local non-governmental organization (NGO) between 2012 and 2014. The NGO used an approach known as community-based adaptation, which puts local people in charge of adapting their communities to the changing climate. This study is, therefore, an evaluation of that approach.
The results of this study show that all six types of intervention—developing climate change awareness, providing weather information, encouraging planting of climate-smart crops, building rainwater harvesting systems, promoting the use of weather-index insurance, and providing cooking stoves with higher fuel efficiency—were effective in helping people adapt to climate change. The researchers also found that the more indicators a project met (out of the ten identified in the study), the more effective it was at helping people adapt. However, increasing the number of indicators that a project includes may not always be feasible, and the researchers note that further research is needed to identify the minimum number of indicators that a project should aim for in order to be effective.
This study is important because it is the first to formally evaluate community-based adaptation. In the past, organizations implementing this approach have not been required to provide information about their projects, for example by publishing their results in scientific journals. This study used a rigorous scientific method to provide an evaluation of this approach that can be used to inform future projects. It also contributes to scientific knowledge of climate change adaptation in several important ways. First of all, it shows that the project took place under real-world conditions, with all the complications that are present in a developing country. Secondly, it is the first study to evaluate different types of intervention. Finally, it develops a method that can be used to evaluate other climate change adaptation projects.
This study was supported by the Norwegian Research Council.
This research is published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology

The researchers also found that the farmers’ decision to plant these varieties was influenced by their location and access to markets, and the availability of water. The study was conducted in 2019 in the dry zones of the semi-arid regions of South Africa, where climate change is intensifying droughts and the frequency of extreme heat.

The researchers collected survey data from 120 farmers in South Africa’s Eastern Cape Province and the Free State, and then conducted 20 in-depth interviews with the farmers. The surveys and interviews asked about farming practices, including which crops farmers planted and why. The researchers then modeled the data and found that farmers were more likely to plant heat-tolerant crops because of the high temperatures in the region. The heat-tolerant crops included maize, the second most important crop in sub-Saharan Africa after maize. The farmers who planted these crops were able to harvest over 1,000 kilograms per hectare, even during droughts, the researchers report.

“Drought is the most important risk to smallholder farmers in the developing world,” study co-author Adoti Kodjo, a researcher at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture in Uganda, says. “Understanding how to help farmers adapt to drought is an important step in increasing their yields and ensuring food security.”

The model the researchers created could help farmers decide which crops to plant based on the climate in their region, Kodjo says. It may also help researchers develop new crop varieties that could help smallholder farmers cope with climate change, he says.

“Crop breeding programs can use this information to prioritize heat and drought tolerance when developing new crop varieties for smallholder farmers in the dry areas of Africa,” Kodjo says.

The research is described in the journal, Science of the Total Environment.

Photo: Jodi Stevens/CIAT

A new way to plan agricultural research

A new method for planning agricultural research and development has been trialled in Tanzania and is now being used in Kenya to ensure that future interventions are aligned with national priorities and meet the needs of farmers.

The method, developed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), and the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF), is called ‘backcasting.’ It is a form of strategic planning that helps researchers and development practitioners identify the key problems they should be addressing in the short term, and the most important long-term issues and priorities.

Tanzania was used as a case study to test the method, and it is now being used in Kenya to identify research topics for the country’s next five-year research strategy. The method is also being used to ensure that on-going research projects are in line with the national strategy.

“By using the backcasting method, researchers and development practitioners can ensure that their interventions are in line with national priorities, and that they are addressing the most pressing issues, and are thus more likely to be relevant, effective, and sustainable,” said Felix Ruti, head of ILRI’s East and Southern Africa program.

The method is designed to help researchers and development practitioners align their work with national and regional strategies, policies, and priorities, and to help them meet the requirements of their different funders.

“We want to make sure that our work is aligned with national strategies and that we are not working in silos,” said Kim Brainwood, head of program coordination at ICRAN. “The backcasting method helps us to work more effectively together and with other sectors such as the forestry department.”

The method can be used at different levels—from the level of a farm to a region or a nation—and is particularly useful for setting the agenda for medium- to long-term research and development interventions.

To use the method, planners list the objectives of various sectors, policies, and strategies and then rate the importance of each objective. They then identify the key problems that must be addressed in the short term (in this case, within the next five years) to meet the objectives and ensure that they are on track. The next step is to identify the long-term issues and priorities that must be addressed in the development of interventions.

Abstract | Full Text


The introduction of non-native species to new environments can have profound negative impacts on native biodiversity and on human societies. Invasive alien species are one of the most severe threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning in South Africa, and a key threat to the survival of vertebrate fauna. In this review, we focus on invasive pathogens as alien species, and discuss the importance of considering both the pathogen and the vertebrate host as components of a species invasion. We used life history information of vertebrate pathogens as invasive species in South Africa to give insights into their potential to spread and harm native biota. We further discuss the importance of collaboration between scientists and managers in managing vertebrate populations when trying to control invasive pathogens.

This is surprising given that many plant and animal invasions are driven by changes in disease epidemiology and that disease is a major component of biological invasions. Here, we examine the history, present status and future research needs of the study of biological invasions caused by disease organisms. We show that invasion science has been constrained by a lack of integration between research on biological and social invasions and by a focus on the introduction of non-indigenous species and their negative consequences, to the exclusion of understanding the facilitative roles that non-native species can play, both directly and indirectly, in causing biological invasions. Gaps in our understanding of disease invasions also reflect knowledge gaps in invasion science more generally. We conclude by identifying research priorities for the study of biological invasions caused by disease organisms, and by arguing that a greater focus on diseases and other pathogens will lead to major advances in invasion science and in the management of biological invasions.

The disease was brought to the continent by Indian traders in the late 1800s, and spread rapidly due to increased movement of people and animals. The virus was so devastating that it became self-limiting, reducing the number of susceptible animals, and then dying out. The last recorded case was in 2001, and the disease has been officially declared eradicated from the continent (except for the Horn of Africa, where the last case was in 2010). The eradication of rinderpest is considered a great success story for both science and international public health cooperation, and is compared to the eradication of smallpox as one of the greatest medical achievements of the 20th century. It is also an example of how a new, more sensitive understanding of epidemiology and ecology can inform control strategies. The main lessons learned include: the value of early intervention; the need to use all available tools including surveillance, vaccination, and quarantine; the importance of a global perspective and the connectivity of animal and human health and the need to integrate social, economic, and ecological factors in the control of diseases. The success of the rinderpest eradication campaign also highlights the fact that political commitment and the involvement of all sectors of society are vital for the success of such campaigns. The first cases of listeriosis — a foodborne illness — were reported in January 2017, but the epidemic didn’t become apparent until five months later.

By summer 2018, 1,000 people had died from the disease and the outbreak was linked to the Polonaise factory of Enterprise Foods in Gauteng, one of the largest food manufacturers in South Africa. The factory was shut down for extensive cleaning and reopened in October 2018.

Listeria is a type of bacteria that can be found in the environment, soil, water and some food products. It is especially common in areas where food is stored or prepared.

The bacteria can cause listeriosis, a rare and sometimes fatal foodborne illness, especially in those with weakened immune systems, pregnant women, the elderly and newborns.

Listeria is part of a group of bacteria called gram-positive bacilli, which look like long, thin rods under a microscope. The bacteria are named after Joseph Lister, a British surgeon who made major advances in antiseptic surgery and is credited with saving many lives.

Listeria is different from E. coli, another type of bacteria that can be found in the environment and in foods. While some strains of E. coli are harmless, others can make you sick and are called “pathogenic.”

“Listeria is one of those pathogens that likes to be in cold places,” said Kathryn Boedigheimer, MS, RDN, a registered dietitian nutritionist and food and health policy specialist at the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

“You would find it in a refrigerator that’s not set at the proper temperature or in an ice cream factory where there’s a leak and listeria is getting into ice cream equipment,” she said.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that each year, 1,600 people are hospitalized due to listeriosis and 260 people die. Pregnant women are 20 times more likely to become infected and have a 40 percent chance of having a miscarriage. In healthy people, listeriosis is treatable with antibiotics.

Invasive species are often used as model organisms in lab experiments. However, the use of invasive species in labs has raised ethical concerns, since invasive species can outcompete or displace native species, and cause a loss of biodiversity. In a commentary published in the open access journal PLOS Biology, on 16 March 2022, scientists propose that the use of invasive species in labs should be banned, and that existing laboratory populations should be humanely euthanized.

Invasive species can cause ecological and economic damage, and can also be harmful to human health. For example, the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) is a known vector for pathogens that cause disease in humans, including Zika, dengue, chikungunya and West Nile virus. This mosquito is now found on every continent except for Antarctica, due to being introduced in the 1980s via used tires.

One of the authors of the commentary, Daniel Rothenberg from Rutgers University in the United States, says “Invasive species are already causing enormous damage to the environment, and are a growing threat to human health. They should not be creating more problems in research labs, where they could potentially escape into the environment and cause even more damage”.

Scientists use invasive species in labs for a variety of reasons. Some invasive species are used as laboratory models because they look similar to, or are closely related to, species being studied for medical purposes. For example, the mouse is a commonly used laboratory rodent, and the fruit fly is another commonly used insect model, in part because mouse and fly genetics are well understood. However, mice and flies are not invasive species. One of the co-authors of the commentary, Konrad Lorenz from the University of Freiburg in Germany, says “The use of invasive species as models in research could be justified if there were no good models available that did not have the potential to escape laboratory conditions. Therefore, before restricting the use of invasive species in research, we need to ensure that suitable non-invasive alternatives for all relevant model organisms are available”.

The Khoekhoe were pastoralists who had kept themselves to a degree separate from the San hunter-gatherers. 

The Khoekhoe kept sheep, goats and sometimes cattle, and they had developed a rich and sophisticated oral tradition, as well as a distinctive body of technological and artistic knowledge. By 1800, they had also developed a unique system of leadership, with a hereditary office known as kgosikgolo, in which a council of elders (kgoro) advised the leader (kgosi). 

But when the Nama people, who were Khoekhoe, split apart over grazing rights during the 18th century, this leadership system was thrown into crisis. The Elisen Vaal drought that followed from 1820 to 1821 pushed the Khoina even further apart. Those who had been allies now became rivals for survival. 

The Khoekhoe had long been marginalised by both the San and the Bantu, and now they were fighting among themselves. It was against this background that the first trekker commandos were able to sign the Khoekhoe up as their allies. 


The Khoekhoe nation had been devastated by inter-tribal fighting and by the Elisen Vaal drought, and they were ready to align with anyone who would help them survive. 


By 1834, many Khoekhoe had become allies of the Voortrekkers, and they were known as the Bondelswarts because the trekkers had given them woolen blankets in exchange for their assistance. But in 1838, the Bondelswarts switched sides and joined the British forces against the Voortrekkers at the Battle of Blood River. 


After the battle, many Bondelswarts settled along the Umgeni River in what is today KwaZulu-Natal, where they still form a small but vibrant part of the local population. But those who stayed in the Cape Colony were marginalised once again, this time by the British. 


In 1925, the Khoikhoi Peoples’ Committee under their leader, Abraham Esau, demanded that the Cape government give them their own country. The committee proposed the territory between the Olifants and Orange Rivers as Khoekhoe-land. But nothing came of it. 

Today, the Khoekhoe and the San survive as two of South Africa’s most resilient cultures. Their struggle for survival continues, but so does their friendship.

Odontogenic Keratocyst (OK) is a relatively rare disorder with cystic appearance having high recurrence rate, derived from the rest of the dental lamina in the mandible and maxilla1. It is also known as Keratocystic Odontogenic Tumor (KOT) or cystic lesion with odontogenic potential2. OK is often misdiagnosed as dentigerous cyst or odontogenic keratocyst3. The age range of OK is from 5 to 60 years old with 20 years as peak incidence, and it shows bimodal distribution. OK is more prevalent in males by a ratio of 1.4:1, and rarely presents before the age of 5 years old3,4.

The clinical behavior of OK is variable and recurrence after complete excision is the main concern5. The reported recurrence rate ranges from 9% to 86% with an average of 43%6-8. The recurrence may be associated with inflammation9, incomplete excision10, cyst wall rupture into the surrounding tissue with cellular changes, tumor infection, or genetic factors11.

The treatment of OK is surgical excision. Wide local excision of OK is recommended to achieve a better outcome and reduce the recurrence rate. However, the precise surgical margin for OK is still under controversy12,13.

The decision tree proposed, which was based on the parameters of size, lesion type, syndromic or solitary nature of the lesion and presence of cortical perforations, would suggest that surgical treatment of the keratocyst is appropriate in most cases. For the cases that are large in size, of a secondary type of lesion, and with cortical perforations, en bloc resection is the recommended treatment. For the rest of the cases, the unbalanced nature of the decision tree would suggest a higher probability of recurrence if treatment is not performed. Thus, early surgical intervention is recommended.

In the past, the standard of care was surgery to remove the tumor, followed by radiation. While this approach was life-saving, it wasn't without adverse effects, as the removal of large parts of the jaw and subsequent radiation therapy can lead to difficulties in opening the mouth, speaking, chewing and even swallowing.
'Our goal is to prevent these severe effects in our patients,' says principal investigator Paul Chaplin, PhD. 'We've shown that hyperbaric oxygen therapy has a beneficial effect on wound healing in animal models of radiation-induced jaw lesions. In this study, we will test the hypothesis that hyperbaric oxygen therapy can successfully prevent the development of jaw lesions in patients who require radiation treatment for head and neck cancer.'
In the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 28 patients will be treated with either hyperbaric oxygen or air while receiving radiation therapy. The patients are randomized to one of two groups: Group 1 receives hyperbaric oxygen therapy while in the hyperbaric chamber and Group 2 receives air. Because the two groups will look the same—both will be in the chamber and both will receive radiation therapy—the researchers are blinded as to which group a patient is in. The patients randomized to the control group will receive the hyperbaric therapy immediately after they complete radiation therapy.
The primary endpoint is the incidence of grade 3 or 4 mucositis (inflammation of the mucous membranes, which can lead to painful mouth ulcers), and the secondary endpoint is the presence of jaw lesions as evidenced by clinical examination and imaging.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy involves breathing 100 percent oxygen while inside a pressurized chamber. This therapy delivers an atmospheric pressure that is two to three times greater than sea level, allowing more oxygen to dissolve in the blood and reach the tissues. Researchers have shown that hyperbaric oxygen therapy can reduce the severity and duration of radiation-induced mucositis.
This study is sponsored by the NCI and is being conducted at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, the University of Washington, MD Anderson Cancer Center, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center and the University of Texas M.D. Anderson Cancer Center.
