A team of researchers led by the University of Birmingham has discovered a new way that T-cells can kill cancer cells. 

The study, published today in Nature Communications, explains how a subset of T-cells, called T-reg, can eliminate cancer by attacking the inside of the tumour from a previously unknown location.

This new research provides hope that new therapies can be developed to treat cancer more effectively. 

T-cells are part of the white blood cells in our immune system that recognise and attack ‘foreign’ bodies such as cancer cells.  However, cancer can often evade these attacks and can grow and spread throughout the body.  In the lab, researchers at the University of Birmingham have identified a new way in which T-cells can eliminate cancer. 

Dr. Michael Thangue, Professor of Molecular Cancer Science at the University of Birmingham, explained: “We discovered that T-reg cells can kill cancer cells by releasing molecules that travel to the inside of the cancer bone and attack from there. 

“This is the first time this mechanism has been observed and it offers new opportunities to treat cancer.  The challenge now is to understand more about how the mechanism works and to determine whether the method has potential to treat other types of cancer.” 

The research was carried out in the lab in cells taken from patients with oral cancer.  The team discovered that a subset of T-cells called T-reg could eliminate cancer cells by releasing molecules called granzyme B and perforin that travel to the inside of the cancer cell and kill it.  The team discovered this by observing the cells under a microscope and by showing that cancer survival was reduced when granzyme B and perforin were not available.  

Dr. Thangue added: “This research is important as it provides a new understanding of how T-cells can eliminate cancer.  We have already identified that this process is dependent on a protein called CXCL10 and that the level of CXCL10 in cancer patients has potential to predict whether a patient’s T-reg are likely to be able to eliminate the cancer.  We are now working to understand more about how the T-reg cells work and whether this mechanism could be used to treat other types of cancer.”

“For patients with large lesions, we need to pay more attention to the cosmetic and functional results,” said Dr. Charles Nduka, a consultant plastic surgeon at the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital (UNTH), Enugu, Nigeria.

Dr. Nduka and his team published their findings in the International Journal of Health Sciences. They noted that the study was limited to examining the cosmetic outcome of the surgery, and not patient satisfaction, which is “an important measure of clinical outcome.”

The researchers also acknowledged that the study group was relatively small, and that the follow-up period was short. They noted that the study was further limited because it involved only one type of surgical procedure.

The researchers evaluated 50 patients who had excision and primary closure of mouth cancer lesions. All the surgeries were performed by Dr. Nduka’s team. The team measured and documented the size of the original lesion in each patient before surgery, and then again after surgery.

The aim of the surgery was to remove the entire cancerous lesion, with a margin of healthy tissue, and to close the surgical site.

The researchers measured the size of the wound after the surgery and then photographed the surgical site. They took the photographs again after 6 weeks of healing.

A total of 44 patients completed the 6-week follow-up. Of these, 27 (61.36%) were males and 17 (38.64%) were females. The age range of the patients was 35–85 years. The mean (average) age was 62.14 years.

The researchers used a cosmetic score chart to assess the surgical outcome. This chart categorizes the cosmetic outcome as poor, fair, good, very good, or excellent.

The researchers found that 7 (15.91%) patients had excellent results; 24 (54.55%) had very good results; 6 (13.64%) had good results; 6 (13.64%) had fair results, and only 1 (2.27%) had poor results.

The patients with excellent and very good scores had lesions that were 2 cm or smaller. The patients with fair scores had lesions between 2 and 4 cm. The patient with a poor score had a lesion that was larger than 4 cm.

The researchers noted that all the patients were able to open their mouths normally after the surgery. However, 6 of them had some restriction of mouth opening because of muscular contracture 6 weeks after surgery. These patients were younger than 50 years.

The first step in the treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis is to get a sputum sample. The sample is then sent to a laboratory for culture and drug-susceptibility testing. The test results are usually available in 2 to 4 weeks. If the samples show that the patient is infected with TB, the doctors will start the patient on a four-drug regimen of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide, for two weeks. This is followed by a four-month course of isoniazid and rifampin. By the end of the six-month treatment, most patients will be cured of their TB. However, some patients may have TB that is resistant to the drugs. These patients will then be placed on a different treatment plan. Doctors may also decide to add more drugs, such as delamanid, to the treatment regimen. If you have questions about your treatment plan, please talk to your doctor or nurse.

samples.ref: Eddagala lya SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV), MERS-CoV ne SARSr-CoV: Okwekaliriza okwokugeraageranya n’ebibalo okusobola okuteesa ebitundu ebiruubirirwa
samples.hyp:
for vaccine design

Keywords: SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, SARSr-CoV, epitopes, vaccine, computational analysis.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 has affected the entire world and resulted in a severe public health crisis. The development of an effective vaccine is one of the top priorities to prevent the spread of the disease. In this study, we performed a comparative epitope mapping analysis using computational methods for three coronaviruses: SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and SARSr-CoV. The results showed that the number of overlapping epitopes between any two of the three viruses was higher than that of non-overlapping epitopes, indicating the presence of cross-reactivity between these viruses. For the design of a universal coronavirus vaccine, we focused on T-cell epitopes that were shared by all three viruses and prioritized epitopes according to their conservation and ability to elicit a strong immune response. We identified 5 candidate epitopes that were highly conserved and presented by multiple human leukocyte antigens (HLAs). The candidate epitopes were also predicted to be binders of T-cell receptors (TCRs) and to be immunogenic in humans. These epitopes may serve as candidate epitopes for the design of a universal coronavirus vaccine. The method described here may be useful for rapid epitope prediction and vaccine design against emerging viruses.

The SARS-CoV and the MERS-CoV, for example, jumped from bats to humans. The virus that causes COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, is zoonotic, that is, it originated in an animal host, most likely an animal sold in a wet market in Wuhan, China. The virus has, however, mutated several times since it first infected humans. This is normal for coronavirus and other RNA viruses. The impact of these mutations on epidemiology and pathogenesis is important to understand to better deal with the disease. Several recent studies have reported the analysis of the genetic evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and its impact on treatment and prevention strategies. In this review, we summarize the current knowledge about the genetic diversity and evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and discuss the implications of the observed changes in the virus’ genetic composition for diagnostic, treatment, and vaccination strategies. We also comment on the effects of mutations on the virus’ host range, replication, virulence, and transmission.


The first genetic variation of SARS-CoV-2 was reported 27 days after the initial description of the novel coronavirus, which occurred in a 55-year-old patient from Wuhan who was admitted to the hospital on December 12, 2019, and died of the disease on February 13, 2020 . This patient was infected with two genetically distinct SARS-CoV-2 strains. The virus was later found to have 15 unique amino acid substitutions, with 13 occurring in the spike (S) protein and two in the envelope (E) protein, which are thought to have arisen from the replication of the original virus in human lung cells . The S protein is the target of most current vaccine efforts and most diagnostic assays; thus, even small changes in its amino acid sequence can have major implications for vaccine design and diagnostic strategies. The rapid and continuous evolution of SARS-CoV-2 poses major challenges for vaccine developers and public health officials. The ability of the virus to evolve may lead to immune escape by the virus, which could potentially result in a treatment or vaccine failure.

The epitope predictions were based on the assessment of the most conserved regions of the parasite and the vaccine candidates by bioinformatics approaches, which included hydrophilicity, antigenicity, and allergenicity analyses, as well as binding predictions to HLA class II molecules by the program PickPocket. Conclusions: There is a need to strengthen the management of malaria and anaemia in pregnancy to reduce adverse pregnancy outcomes.

The study aimed to present the pooled estimates of prevalence and risk factors of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.

This systematic review and meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. A search was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS for studies reporting the prevalence of arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19, up to January 2021. The search was restricted to human studies conducted in inpatients with confirmed COVID-19. The risk of bias of the included studies was assessed using the Robins I2 statistic. The main outcomes were prevalence of new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF), supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), ventricular tachycardia (VT), and ventricular fibrillation (VF) in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.

Of 423 identified articles, 10 studies were included in the review. The prevalence of new-onset AF, SVT, VT, and VF in patients with COVID-19 were 3.8% (95% CI, 2.6–5.4%), 2.2% (95% CI, 1.3–3.3%), 1.1% (95% CI, 0.6–1.8%), and 0.6% (95% CI, 0.3–1.1%), respectively. There was high heterogeneity among the studies for the estimates of prevalence of AF (I2 = 88.6%), SVT (I2 = 89.2%), VT (I2 = 96.2%), and VF (I2 = 0.0%). Patients with a history of cardiovascular disease had 8.2-fold higher prevalence of new-onset AF (95% CI, 2.2–30.8%) compared to those without. Hospitalized patients with COVID-19 had an increased risk of developing new-onset AF (OR 5.47, 95% CI 2.36–12.74) and VT (OR 6.25 95% CI, 2.37–16.45) when compared to the general population.

Our study aimed to summarize the current understanding of the prevalence, clinical characteristics, pathophysiology, and management of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients. Most of the studies revealed a high incidence of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients, especially in those who required intensive care unit (ICU) admission and were supported by mechanical ventilation. The most common arrhythmias were new-onset bradycardia and new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF), followed by ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF). Some patients experienced multiple types of arrhythmias. Patients with arrhythmia were more likely to have a history of cardiovascular disease, higher levels of creatine kinase (CK) and D-dimer, lower levels of lymphocyte, and lower levels of platelet. Moreover, some patients with cardiac arrhythmia developed heart failure and required cardiac catheterization, implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) implantation, and cardiothoracic surgery. Additionally, patients with AF and VT/VF had a higher risk of mortality. Several mechanisms were proposed to explain the occurrence of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients, including inflammation, arrhythmogenic triggers, oxidative stress, hypoxia, and modulation of ion channels. For the management of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients, some studies suggested amiodarone as the first-line treatment, while others recommended conventional antiarrhythmic drugs and heart rate control. Moreover, cardiac mechanical support and cardiothoracic surgery were performed in patients with cardiac arrhythmia and heart failure. In a word, cardiac arrhythmia is common and carries a high risk of mortality in COVID-19 patients, especially in those with advanced disease and heart failure. AF and VT/VF were more likely to occur than bradycardia. Timely diagnosis and appropriate management of cardiac arrhythmia are very important for the prognosis of COVID-19 patients. More large-sample studies with long-term follow-up are needed to explore the exact incidence and mechanisms of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients.

We aimed to develop and validate a deep learning system for detecting and classifying arrhythmias using electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings. This work could facilitate the early detection of arrhythmias and their classification, which would be beneficial for the management of patients with cardiovascular diseases. We developed and validated a deep learning–based arrhythmia detection and classification model for 10,000 ECG recordings (9,820 for training and validation and 180 for testing). Our model can accurately detect arrhythmias with a sensitivity of 0.96 and a negative predictive value of 0.99 and classify them into 8 arrhythmia classes. Our model yields a prediction within 0.01 seconds and has potential for use with wearable technology. The deep learning–based model outperformed other machine learning–based comparison models. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset with multiclass classification of arrhythmias and the first ECG-based model that can detect and classify arrhythmias in this scale. Although the model was validated, external validation and long-term follow-up are needed. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaixujia/arrhythmia-detection-and-classification.

Many Covid-19 patients had irregular heartbeats during infection

Many Covid-19 patients had irregular heartbeats during infection. Photo: Shutterstock

New research shows that a large proportion of Covid-19 patients were affected by an irregular heartbeat. This is a condition known as atrial fibrillation, which can lead to blood clots.

Many patients who were admitted to the hospital with Covid-19 had an irregular heartbeat during their infection. This is shown by a recent study that has followed more than 61,000 patients. The condition is known as atrial fibrillation, which can lead to blood clots. Among those who were admitted to the hospital, one in five had atrial fibrillation. The condition is also known to increase the risk of stroke.

Follows previous research

The study is an extension of two previous studies that also had follow-ups with more than 14,000 patients. These studies were conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and several other universities and hospitals in Sweden.

“We followed the patients for a year and found that atrial fibrillation occurred in 7.5 percent of all Covid-19 patients. This is five percent more than in the general population, which means that the patients were 1.5 times more likely to be affected by atrial fibrillation than other people,” says MD, PhD, Olof Stråman, researcher at the Department of Clinical Science, Intervention and Bioengineering at Karolinska Institutet.

Can lead to blood clots

Atrial fibrillation is the most common type of irregular heartbeat and is characterized by an abnormal electrical activity in the upper heart chambers (atria). The condition leads to the heart not being able to pump blood as efficiently as it should, which can lead to blood clots. The clots can travel to other parts of the body and cause a stroke.

The risk of stroke is already high among Covid-19 patients. That so many of them also had atrial fibrillation is therefore a major finding of the study.

“We already know that Covid-19 affects the lungs and that it can lead to a severe inflammatory reaction in the body. Our results indicate that the infection also affects the heart and that this is a common and significant finding,” says Olof Stråman.

The study is published in the scientific journal Open Heart.

Source: Karolinska Institutet

ECGs are tests that record the electrical activity of the heart. They can also detect potentially dangerous heart rhythms.

Arrhythmias were seen in 18% of the Covid-19 patients admitted to hospital, compared to 3% of the other patients. After taking into account other factors, such as age, existing heart conditions, and sex, the researchers still observed a two-fold increase in arrhythmias in the Covid-19 group compared to those admitted for other reasons.

While most of the arrhythmias were mild and resolved without treatment, the researchers say that about 1 in 5 patients had more severe arrhythmias that required treatment.

samples.src: In this chapter, we provide a review of empirical studies conducted on PTSD, mental health and wellbeing of migrants.
samples.ref: Mu ssuula eno, twetegereza okunoonyereza okwakolebwa ku PTSD, embeera y’ebirowoozo n’okubeera obulungi okw’abawaŋŋanguka.
samples.hyp:
We begin by examining the impact of migration on the mental health and wellbeing of migrants. We then review the empirical evidence on the association between PTSD and mental health and wellbeing outcomes in migrants. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for policy and future research.

The impact of migration on the mental health and wellbeing of migrants

There is a large and growing body of empirical evidence showing that migration has both positive and negative effects on mental health and the psychological wellbeing of migrants (e.g. Leung et al. 2014; Silove 2006; Silove et al. 2007). However, the direction and extent of these effects can vary depending on individual, cultural and other factors (e.g. Kyrios et al. 2018; Leung et al. 2014; Silove 2006; Silove et al. 2007). In this section, we provide a brief review of the empirical evidence on the impact of migration on the mental health and wellbeing of migrants. Table 6.2 summarizes the studies we review in this section.

As shown in Table 6.2, research has examined the impact of migration on the mental health and wellbeing of migrants across different populations, including resettled refugees (e.g. Porter and Haslam 2005), asylum seekers (e.g. De Silva et al. 2005), documented and undocumented migrants (e.g. Kira et al. 2019), and international students (e.g. Ward and Jones 1999). These studies have found that migration can impact the mental health and wellbeing of migrants in a number of ways, including through exposure to traumatic events, changes in social support, enculturation in a new culture, and changes in socioeconomic status.

One way in which migration can impact the mental health and wellbeing of migrants is through exposure to traumatic events. Traumatic events can include a range of experiences, such as natural disasters, war, persecution, and torture. Exposure to traumatic events has been shown to increase the risk of developing PTSD (e.g. Brewin et al. 2017). As shown in Table 6.2, several studies have examined the impact of exposure to traumatic events on the mental health and wellbeing of migrants. For example, Porter and Haslam (2005) found that resettled refugees reported higher levels of trauma symptoms compared to the general population. Similarly, Kira et al. (2019) found that undocumented migrants in the USA reported higher levels of trauma symptoms compared to both US-born individuals

However, a few studies have investigated the impact of stressors in different migration phases. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the impact of a wide range of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health and PTSD of a community-based sample of 505 Arab refugees resettled in the third country. This cross-sectional study used a structured questionnaire that included the Syrian Refugee Stressor Questionnaire (SRSQ) and the Symptom Checklist-90-Revised (SCL-90-R). The SRSQ was developed specifically for this study and assessed the stressors refugees experienced in 11 pre- and 5 post-migration domains. The SCL-90-R is a validated screening tool for mental health. The analysis included bivariate and multivariate logistic regression. Almost half of the participants (48.9%) reported subclinical to clinical levels of PTSD and more than half (56.1%) reported severe mental health distress. In bivariate analysis, experiencing stressors in all 16 domains was significantly associated with severe mental health distress and PTSD, except for the belongingness domain. In multivariate analysis, results supported associations between severe mental health distress and PTSD and stressors in 13 out of 16 domains. Severe mental health distress and PTSD were particularly strongly associated with stressors in the domains of family separation, death of a loved one, personal safety, belongingness, and sexual and gender-based violence. The study highlights the need to develop and employ interventions that target multiple stressors across the entire migration process to improve the mental health of refugees.

In Libya, a common transit country, a large number of refugees and migrants face trauma, torture, and various forms of abuse including forced labour, forced military recruitment, extortion, and sexual abuse and exploitation.

The study, conducted in cooperation with the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Libyan National Cancer Research Centre, has shown that 73% of migrants and 36% of refugees had their first cancer diagnosis within five years of arriving in Europe. The most common types of cancer were digestive system and respiratory organ cancers. The study underlines the need for early detection of cancer in migrants and refugees that arrive in Europe with a history of cancer risk factors from their country of origin.

The researchers also found that 47% of migrants did not access mental health services, as they were afraid of authorities’ reactions, faced language barriers, or had to overcome negative stereotypes. To improve the mental health of migrants, the researchers suggest to increase access to comprehensive primary health care, including mental health care and social support. In addition, authorities and receiving communities should offer housing, education, and employment to facilitate social integration and reduce social exclusion.

These psychological issues are prevalent in all regions of the world, however, the prevalence of these conditions is higher in developing countries compared to developed countries. In addition, the prevalence rates of depression, anxiety and PTSD in Africa are higher than those reported in other parts of the world. Social support was found to buffer the effects of stress on psychological well-being, and coping mechanisms served as buffers between potentially toxic working conditions and psychological well-being. samples.src: Refugee mental health affected by the situation left behind and settling in a new place
samples.ref: Embeera y’ebirowoozo by’ababundabunda ekosebwa embeera gye balesse ewaka n’okusenga mu kifo ekipya
samples.hyp:
The situation that refugees flee from and the difficulties in settling in their new environment can have a negative impact on their mental health. (Unsplash/Janice Zhang)

A new study by Umeå University in Sweden has shown that refugees’ mental health is affected by both the situation they flee from and the difficulties in settling in their new environment. The study was carried out in cooperation with psychiatrists at the Umeå Regional Hospital and was published in the scientific journal BMC Psychiatry.

“Our results indicate that both exposure to traumatic events in their country of origin and post-migration stress are important to consider when assessing the mental health of refugees. The higher the level of exposure, the more severe the symptoms”, says Pontus Åström, PhD student at the Department of Clinical Science.

For his master’s thesis in psychiatry, Åström has analysed data from the Swedish Barometer Study, a study that follows refugees who have arrived in Sweden and looks at their social relationships, mental and physical health. This particular analysis is the first to look at which factors are related to mental health problems in refugees who have been resettled in Sweden two years after their arrival.

The results show that both pre-migration traumatic experiences and post-migration difficulties are related to mental health. Pre-migration exposure was analysed by asking refugees how many traumatic experiences they had been exposed to in their country of origin. These experiences included war and violence, violence because of the refugees’ ethnicity, human rights violations, and natural disasters. Many refugees were exposed to several different types of traumatic experiences.

“It is important to ask refugees about their experiences in their home country. It is not enough to ask about and focus on the journey they have taken”, says Åström.

Post-migration stress was analysed by asking the refugees how difficult they had found it to settle in their new environment. They were asked to focus on factors such as language, lack of social connections, lack of financial resources, and lack of housing. Refugees who had experienced more traumatic events both in their home country and in their new environment had the most severe symptoms.

It is not possible to prevent all traumatic experiences, but increased support during integration could have a positive impact. The results could also be used to identify refugees who need support.

“The results could be used to develop methods to identify which refugees need support. Not all refugees need help, so it is important to find a method to target those who need it”, says Åström.

Photo | AFP

More than 90% of migrants who attempt to cross the Mediterranean to reach Europe are men. But women and children make up a significant proportion of those who get there, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

The IOM has launched a new report, based on data from the first half of 2018, which highlights the experiences of women and children migrants in the Mediterranean.

The report shows that of the 113,054 migrants who arrived in Italy by sea between January and June this year, 12% were women and 23% were children.

According to the IOM, 2,877 women and 5,348 children were rescued from boats in the Mediterranean and landed in Italy between January and June this year.

The IOM’s chief of mission in Italy, Francesca Fontanini, said: “Women and children migrants are a particularly vulnerable group. They face specific gender-based risks along the whole migration route, which often go undetected or unrecorded.”

The book, titled “African Migration to Europe: A Cultural Ethnography”, is published by Routledge, and can be ordered online.

The study, which was conducted by Dr. Catherine Hough, Dr. Catherine Campbell, Ms. Nana Asamoah Asare, and Professor Michaela Hoffmann-Riem, focused on Ghanaian and Zimbabwean migrants living in the city of Leipzig, in eastern Germany.

The researchers used in-depth interviews and focus group discussions to explore how the migrants conceptualised HIV and how this changed over time. The concept of HIV was analysed using a ‘cultural ethnography’ framework, which considers how the meaning of HIV is constructed in different cultural contexts.

The study found that the migrants’ ideas about HIV and AIDS changed when they moved from South Africa to Germany. This was because South Africa has one of the highest HIV prevalences in the world (11.2% among the age group 15–49), while the prevalence in Germany is less than 0.1%. As a result, the migrants found it difficult to relate to HIV risk talk in Germany, and some of them actually reduced their HIV risk behaviours.

However, the migrants’ ideas about HIV and AIDS were also shaped by their local contexts in Leipzig. For example, some of the migrants engaged in street commerce and therefore had contact with a lot of different people, which increased their risk of acquiring HIV. In response to this, the researchers say that HIV prevention interventions should be tailored to the unique needs of migrants, and should be implemented in collaboration with local authorities in order to be effective.

The study concluded by calling for more research to better understand the complex interplay between global, national, and local contexts and how these shape the unique risks that African migrants face when accessing health care in high-income countries.

samples.hyp:
Heartwater is caused by the protozoan parasite, Cardia Olympica, which is transmitted by the brown dog tick, Amblyomma hebraeum. The brown dog tick is a cosmopolitan species and is found in tropical and subtropical regions of the world. In Africa, it is an important vector of Heartwater. The brown dog tick has a high propensity for maintaining infective forms of the parasite, and for transmitting the parasite to the tick vector, Rhipicephalus evertsi, under laboratory conditions. The brown dog tick is a three-host tick, requiring two bloodmeals, one from a small mammal and the other from a large mammal, for the completion of its life cycle. The brown dog tick has a high propensity for man as a host, and is able to complete its life cycle on this host, as well as on a variety of other hosts of different sizes and species. In this study, the authors collected ticks from dogs in the southern district of Botswana, and determined the infection rates of A. hebraeum and C. olimpica. They also determined the effects of the brown dog tick on the growth of Trypanosoma congolense, the agent of African Animal Trypanosomiasis or Nagana. The authors found that a high infection rate of the brown dog tick, together with the presence and persistence of the heartwater parasite, resulted in a high prevalence of heartwater in dogs. The authors also found that the presence of the brown dog tick, on the host, resulted in a high infection rate of T. congolense in the vector, Rhipicephalus evertsi. In addition, in tick-bite experiments, they found that the brown dog tick enhanced the infectivity of T. congolense to R. evertsi. The authors concluded that the presence and persistence of the brown dog tick, A. hebraeum, augments the burden of heartwater in the southern district of Botswana, by facilitating the transmission of heartwater, from dog to dog, and from dog to other large mammals that serve as hosts for R. evertsi.

A total of 1180 animals (cattle, sheep, goats and pigs) were examined for the presence of heartwater. In addition, ticks were counted and identified from 210 cattle. Heartwater was diagnosed based on the presence of parasites in the peripheral blood smear. The overall prevalence of heartwater was 3.4% (n=40). The adjusted prevalence for cattle was 3.8% and for small ruminants (sheep and goats) it was 2.3%. The prevalence for cattle was 4.7% in Ngwaketse and 0.7% in Tawana. The prevalence of heartwater was not significantly associated with age or body condition of the animals. In conclusion, this study has shown that heartwater is present in Botswana and that the parasite is endemic in the soft tick-infested areas. The prevalence is low when compared to other African countries.

samples.hyp: The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of A. hebraeum on cattle in the Southern District of Botswana. A total of 1,152 cattle from 48 villages in the Southern District were examined for the presence of A. hebraeum ticks between October and November 2000. Ticks were collected and identified to the species level. The prevalence of A. hebraeum was determined for each village and mapped. The overall prevalence of female A. hebraeum on cattle in the Southern District of Botswana was 26.9% (305/1,141). The prevalence of A. hebraeum varied significantly (P < 0.0001) between the study areas. The area immediately north of the Molopo River had the highest prevalence of A. hebraeum (59.3%); followed by the areas to the north and south of this area. The area around Jwaneng had the least prevalence (0.2%). Blood samples were collected from 1150 cattle, 360 sheep, and 355 goats from 44 farms in the study area. Point of care testing is a convenient approach to testing that can be used to get fast and reliable results on various diseases and health conditions. However, there are still barriers to the technology that prevent its wider use.

The Challenges of Point of Care Testing

Point of care testing, also known as near patient testing or point-of-use testing, is testing that is performed at or near the location where the patient is being cared for. This is in contrast to laboratory testing, where the sample is sent to a separate location for testing.

Point of care tests are tests that can be performed by non-professional personnel, such as nurses or doctors, without the need for specialized equipment or training. They are designed to be quick, easy to use, and provide results in a timely manner.

There are many advantages of point of care testing. These include:

  • Increased convenience for patients, as they do not need to travel to a laboratory for testing.
  • Quicker results, which can help to inform treatment decisions more quickly.
  • Reduced risk of sample contamination, as samples do not need to be transported to a separate location.
  • Ability to perform testing in remote or underserved areas, where access to a laboratory may be limited.

Despite these advantages, point of care testing also has some disadvantages. These include:

  • A lack of regulation, which can lead to inaccurate or misleading results.
  • Limited availability of tests, particularly in developing countries.
  • High cost of tests, which can make them unaffordable for some patients.
  • A lack of evidence for the clinical effectiveness of some point of care tests.

Overcoming the Barriers to Point of Care Testing

Despite the challenges, there are initiatives aimed at overcoming the barriers to point of care testing. One example is the work of the Diagnostics for All program, which is a global initiative that aims to make accurate, low-cost diagnostic tests widely available in low-resource settings.

Another example is the use of mobile health (mHealth) technologies, which can be used to perform point of care tests remotely. For example, a smartphone connected to a special sensor can be used to test for diseases such as malaria or HIV.

However, there are still barriers to the wider use of point of care testing. In India and South Africa, for example, there are concerns about the accuracy of point of care tests and a lack of trained personnel to perform the tests.

However, the implementation of POC testing has been slow. One reason for this is that the tests are often not designed with the user in mind. To address this issue, we used a human-centered design (HCD) approach to develop a low-cost, easy-to-use, handheld malaria diagnostic device. In this study, we describe the user experience and evaluate the acceptability of the device in a community setting in Entebbe, Uganda. A total of 190 participants between the ages of 18 and 35 years old were recruited. Participants were asked to complete a survey, which included demographic questions, questions regarding their experience with health care in Uganda, and questions related to their experience with the malaria diagnostic device. The majority of participants (84.7%) reported ever having to travel to a health center or hospital because of illness. More than half (56.8%) reported that they had to travel more than 5 km, with 26.3% traveling more than 10 km. A little over half of the participants (50.8%) were satisfied with their most recent visit to a health center or hospital. The most common reasons for dissatisfaction were long wait times (27.7%) and difficulty communicating with health care workers (20.5%). The majority of participants reported that they would be comfortable using a malaria diagnostic device (86.3%). The reasons for comfort use were to save time (“to avoid queuing” 47.4% and “to get results quickly” 43.9%) and to get reliable results (“to get accurate results” 59.5% and “to avoid visiting multiple times because of inaccurate results” 9.7%). The most common preferred languages to use with the malaria diagnostic device were English (68.4%) and Luganda (63.5%). Overall, participants reported that they would use the malaria diagnostic device if it was available (86.8%) and that they would be willing to pay for its use (85.8%). Our findings suggest that community members in Uganda are in need of a malaria diagnostic device that is not only accurate but also easy to use and cost-effective. The HCD approach is useful for developing diagnostic tests that are user-friendly and may lead to an increase in acceptability and uptake of diagnostic tests in low- and middle-income countries.

The research design was based on an applied, contextual and participatory understanding of qualitative research as described by Büscher et al. (2012). The research team included an experienced qualitative researcher (Arunima Jati), a medical doctor with significant experience in public health and the implementation of POC testing in India (A. S. Singh), and a social scientist with experience in conducting qualitative research in community settings in South Africa (Tanya van Oosterom). The project was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Research Ethics Committee of the Nuffield Centre for Health and Social Care at the University of Leeds, the Indian Council of Medical Research, and the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of KwaZulu-Natal. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. In India, the study was conducted in the rural area of a district in the eastern state of Orissa. In both countries, semi-structured interviews were conducted with key informants (health administrators, medical officers, laboratory technicians) and patients. In India, 12 interviews were conducted with patients in three villages, two in each village. In South Africa, 20 interviews were conducted with patients in four villages, five in each village. In India, 14 interviews were conducted with key informants in the district headquarters, which included one interview each with the district magistrate, the civil surgeon (a medical doctor who is also the district administrator), the block medical officer, the state quality assurance consultant for POC testing, the state coordinator for point-of-care CD4 testing, and eight interviews with medical officers and laboratory technicians. In South Africa, 12 interviews were conducted with key informants at a clinic in a rural area, which included one interview each with the provincial health department representative, the clinic manager, a medical officer, and the laboratory manager, and seven interviews with laboratory technicians. The quality of point-of-care testing (POCT) is putting a strain on the healthcare of South Africa and India, according to a recent study published in The Lancet Global Health.

POCT is a system of testing patients outside of hospital settings, and has been proven to be a cost-effective method of monitoring and diagnosing conditions. However, the system is not without its flaws. The study found that the poor quality of POCT in South Africa and India is causing a delay in patient care.

In South Africa, only 34% of patients were tested for HIV within one hour of arrival at the hospital. In India, only 17% of patients were tested for tuberculosis within one hour of arrival. This delay in testing is putting patients at risk for developing further complications from their conditions.

The study also found that the poor quality of POCT is causing a strain on the healthcare system. In South Africa, only 52% of hospitals were able to provide POCT services to their patients. In India, only 27% of hospitals were able to provide POCT services.

The quality of POCT is essential for providing quality healthcare to patients. Poor POCT is putting a strain on the healthcare system in South Africa and India, and is causing a delay in patient care. More investment is needed in POCT to improve the quality of healthcare for patients in these countries.

The authors of the study are from the University of Cape Town, the University of KwaZulu-Natal, the University of Witwatersrand, the University of California, and the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health.

The article is titled "The state of point-of-care testing in South Africa and India: a cross-sectional study of availability, costs and quality."

The term point-of-care is also used to refer to the actual device or instrument used to perform the test. The use of POC tests can improve patient care in many ways, including reducing the time to get test results, enabling healthcare providers to monitor patients more closely, and empowering patients to take a more active role in their own care. POC tests can also be less expensive than sending samples to a laboratory, and they can be easier to use, especially in remote or resource-limited settings. Some common examples of POC tests include blood glucose monitoring for diabetic patients, urine pregnancy tests, and rapid STI screenings. Overall, POC tests are a valuable tool in modern medicine, offering convenience, cost savings, and improved patient outcomes.

The use of POC tests in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) can be particularly beneficial, as they can help to overcome challenges related to distant or limited reference laboratories. However, implementing POC tests in these countries requires careful planning and consideration of factors such as test accuracy, reagent stability, storage and transportation requirements, and the need for trained personnel. It is important to select POC tests that are appropriate for the local context and have been validated in LMICs. With appropriate implementation, POC tests can provide accurate and timely results, reducing the need for patients to travel for testing and enabling earlier intervention and treatment.

samples.hyp:
The aim of this study was to understand why patients are referred to other hospitals and to identify the problems that arise when patients are referred. This was a cross-sectional study conducted at the main campus of the University of Gondar from March to May 2012. A sample of 200 patients referred to other hospitals was taken from the medical wards of the hospital. A semi-structured questionnaire interview was used to collect the data. The majority of the patients (96.5%) were referred to the regional hospital. The major reasons for referral were to improve the diagnostic capacity (37.5%) and to improve the treatment facility (28.5%). The problems arising from referral were that it was time consuming (52.5%) and was difficult for the patients (32.5%). This study showed that the majority of the patients were referred to the regional hospital and the referral was mainly for improving the diagnostic and treatment facilities. The referral was time consuming and difficult for the patients. There is a need to provide diagnostic and treatment facilities in the hospital itself.

This is because the methods used are not standardised. For example, in one lab, one method may be used to test the first 100 samples, and a different method may be used for the remaining 100 samples. This is not acceptable. 

The following is a list of the most common methods used by the labs. 

1. Rapid test using a cassette
2. Rapid test using a lateral flow device
3. Chemiluminescence assay with a microparticle immunoassay
4. Chemiluminescence assay with a rapid test using a lateral flow device
5. Immunochromatography
6. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
7. Western blotting
8. PCR

The first two methods are not reliable because they are prone to giving false positive results. A false positive result means that the test reports a person as HIV positive when in actual fact the person is not infected with HIV. This is a very big problem in Zambia because it means that many HIV-negative people are told that they are HIV positive. Some of these people are then started on ARVs, but in actual fact, they don’t need them. Starting people on ARVs when they don’t need them is very expensive, and it can cause severe side effects, which can be life-threatening. 

The last three methods are very reliable. They are standardised, which means that they are run in a consistent manner. For example, if a lab uses western blotting to test 200 samples, it will use the same western blotting method for all 200 samples. This is good because it increases the reliability of the test results. 

The third method is slightly more reliable than the immunochromatography and ELISA methods because it has a higher sensitivity. 

The second most reliable method is chemiluminescence with a rapid test using a lateral flow device. This method is highly standardised, which is why it is the most reliable. 

Please note that no matter how reliable the method used, if it is not performed properly, then the results may still be wrong. For example, if someone who is not a trained technician performs western blotting, the results will most likely be wrong. 

Please note that the purpose of this article is just to give an overview of the reliability of the different HIV testing methods used by the labs. For each method, there are many factors that can influence how reliable the results are. This article doesn’t discuss these factors.

Of these, 90 persons were contacted after one year and asked about their experiences of the visit to the clinic. "It was shown that the patients' experiences of the visit to the clinic were good. They were satisfied with the treatment they were offered, but they had many questions that had not been answered when they were at the clinic. They also wanted to have follow-up meetings, but were not always sure whether they would be offered one or not," says Maria Hellman, doctor and doctoral student at the Department of Infectious Disease Control at the Karolinska Institutet. "The patients described that they tried to prepare for the future by looking for information about HIV on the Internet. When they did not find the answers to their questions, they became more anxious and some also described that they had tried to get the test with a different identity card because they lived too far from the clinic or because they did not wanted to take an anonymous test. This caused additional problems since the patients then sometimes did not get the follow-up meetings that they needed." HIV testing in Sweden is voluntary and completely anonymous. There are 25 clinics around the country that can test for HIV. There are also a number of other clinics in the capital city Stockholm. The researchers want to use their findings to improve the follow-up of new patients. "It is important that the clinics offer the patients more information about HIV and that they offer more follow-up meetings. The content of the visit also needs to be adapted so that patients can get answers to their questions and feel safe and secure and have fewer reasons to be anxious," says Maria Hellman. She points out that it is important for the patients to get the right advice and information in order to be able to make healthy choices. "The patients' experiences and opinions are important and need to be considered so that we can offer all patients the best possible care."

Annals of Intensive Care volume 8, Article number: 77 (2018)

Published: 3 September 2018

We used Maxfield and Babbie’s (2015) concept analysis as a methodological study to explore, describe and define the concepts of critical illness and critical care. This paper presents the first phase of the concept analysis, which includes the preliminary steps prior to delimiting the concept.

A conceptual analysis was conducted of 44 relevant, peer-reviewed papers describing the concepts’ application in intensive care units (ICUs). Most articles were published in the last decade, with only a few papers published before 2000. The majority of papers were written by authors from Europe or North America. Qualitative content analysis was conducted, with the first author coding the text in NVIVO. The initial codes were grouped into categories, and subcategories, with the help of a clinical physiologist and two critical care physicians. Finally, a summary table was constructed, highlighting the attributes that defined each concept. “Critical illness” was defined in terms of an acute, often sudden, worsening of pre-existing disease, or the development of a new disease, leading to severe impairment in daily functioning, and often, multi-organ failure. “Critical care” was defined as the early, organised and systematic treatment of the most seriously ill. This is usually provided by a specialist team, and includes close monitoring, support for all organ systems, and risk assessment. The concepts are distinct in that critical illness is a patient description, based on functional outcome, whereas critical care is a unit and organisational description, based on the provision of care. This study has highlighted the complexity of the concepts’ use and application. There is a need for common definitions of these concepts, to enable improved research, education and collaboration.

The Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) defined the term "critical illness" as a life-threatening illness requiring intensive care. The term "critical care" was defined as the specialty of medicine addressing the acute and life-threatening care of a patient. The American Hospital Association published a report in 1976 which defined a CCU as an area within a hospital where patients with acute potentially life-threatening medical and/or surgical conditions were cared for under direct physician supervision. The report did not define the specific services a CCU was to provide, but required that within the CCU, medical and surgical patients be cared for by physicians who were board certified in either internal medicine, surgery, or a related field, under the direct supervision of a board certified internist, surgeon, or related specialty. A committee of the American College of Critical Care Medicine (ACCM) reported in 1983 that a patient should be considered a candidate for CCU care if the patient met one or more of 15 criteria. The most recent ACCM committee report in 2003 defined seven criteria that would support a patient's placement in a CCU.

The first definition of a CCU was published in 1975 by the American Hospital Association (AHA). This report was developed by a task force within the AHA's Board on Medical Education and was designed to assist hospitals in the organization of inpatient care. The report described the CCU as an area within a hospital where patients with acute potentially life-threatening medical and/or surgical conditions were cared for under direct physician supervision. The report did not define the specific services a CCU was to provide, but required that within the CCU, medical and surgical patients be cared for by physicians who were board certified in either internal medicine, surgery, or a related field, under the direct supervision of a board certified internist, surgeon, or related specialty. The report identified 15 criteria that a patient had to meet to be considered a candidate for CCU care. These criteria were not intended to exclude patients from CCU care, but rather to define a patient population that would likely benefit from CCU care. The 15 criteria were as follows:

1.     Patient is a surgical patient or postoperative patient who meets one or more of the following criteria:

        1.     Mechanical ventilation.

        2.     Cardiac arrest.

        3.     Hypotension unresponsive to fluid and/or vasoactive drugs.

samples.hyp:
The major strength of this study is that it is the first to examine the association between PM and HbA1c levels in children with type 1 diabetes. The study is also limited by its single-center design, which limits the ability to generalize the results to other centers, and the relatively small sample size which increases the risk of type I error. In addition, glycated hemoglobin was measured only once in our study, even though multiple measurements over time could have provided more information about the long-term effects of PM on HbA1c levels. Finally, this is an observational study and therefore we cannot establish a causal relationship between PM and HbA1c levels. It is possible that unmeasured confounders, or variables that were not accounted for in the analysis, may be causing the observed associations. However, the strength of the associations in our study, even after adjustment for potential confounders, suggests that PM does play a role in modulating HbA1c levels in children with type 1 diabetes.

In phase 2, a review of the nursing literature from 1993 to 1997 revealed 65 additional articles, published after the initial analysis, that referenced the concepts of critical care or critical illness. These articles were analyzed for common definitions and uses of the 2 concepts. Results of phase 1 revealed that critical care was defined in terms of physical location and level of technology. The concept of critical care was defined in 5 categories and 11 subcategories. The predominant use of critical care was found to be in terms of physical location. All articles defined critical illness in terms of severity of disease. The concept of critical illness was defined in 3 categories and 14 subcategories. The predominant use of critical illness was in reference to the severity of disease and organ dysfunction. The re-definition of “critically ill” patients and their care has been published in the Journal of Critical Care. The paper is titled “A proposed unit of care for patients who are ‘not quite’ critically ill: a new definition and model of care.”

The paper was published online on May 6, 2021, and will be published in the June 2021, print version of the Journal of Critical Care.

The paper’s corresponding author is M. Palmer, who is a PhD Student and Research Assistant in the Division of Cardiology at the University of Utah. Co-authors are J. Carne, M. Broughey, B. Clark, S. Chong, A. Szerlip, and J. P. Byrne, who are all affiliated with the University of Utah.

The paper has been published online at https://www.jcriticalcare.com

Abstract

Background: There is a lack of consistency in how patients are defined and treated in hospital wards and intensive care units (ICUs). This lack of consistency leads to over and under treatment of patients. A patient who is not quite critically ill may be admitted to an ICU, where the resources required for their care may be inappropriate for their illness. Alternatively, a patient who is critically ill may not be admitted to an ICU due to limited capacity, where the resources required for their care are required for a patient who would have a higher likelihood of death without ICU support. This may lead to under treatment of a patient who would otherwise have had a better chance at survival with the care they required.

Purpose: The purpose of this paper is to define a new category of hospital patients, who we propose be called “severely ill” patients, and to propose a model of care for these patients.

The study, led by researchers at the University of Oxford and the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Oxford Biomedical Research Centre (BRC), shows that implementing a set of standardised definitions used by all healthcare professionals worldwide could help improve the care of patients who are very unwell and require urgent care.

The international DELPHI study involved 1,000 hospitals in 35 countries. It provides the first large-scale evidence that using a standard approach, based on a shared understanding of key terms, can improve the consistency of decisions about patients and communication between members of the healthcare team. 

The study is published today in The Lancet, the leading international medical journal.

During the DELPHI study, researchers developed 45 standardised definitions of terms used in the care of patients in emergency situations, including shock, life-threatening low blood pressure, serious infection, futility and palliative care. The definitions were agreed by a large group of clinicians from different countries.

In the Oxford study, published today in The Lancet, researchers examined the impact of using the standardised definitions on patient outcomes at a large hospital in Cape Town. 

The hospital’s emergency department saw approximately 600 patients a month who were so unwell that they required urgent care to be stabilised and then transferred to other parts of the hospital for further treatment. These patients are at risk of death or disability and often require long periods of treatment and rehabilitation.

After the implementation of the standardised definitions, the researchers examined the impact on the treatment decisions and outcomes for 1,301 patients. 

The results show that use of the standard definitions resulted in more consistent treatment decisions and improved communication between different members of the healthcare team. The current definition of critical illness—being at risk of dying from an illness—is problematic, according to a new paper published online on May 20, 2020, in the journal Intensive Care Medicine. 

The paper’s authors argue that this definition leaves out the experiences of critically ill patients who survive their illness and suggest a new definition: “a severe acute illness with a high risk of mortality and a substantial likelihood of severe long-term sequelae or death, even if treated”.

The new definition aims to better reflect the experiences of patients and their families. In addition to the risk of death, the authors want to draw attention to the potential for patients to suffer long-term health issues as a result of their critical illness. 

To illustrate their point, the authors point to data from the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) and Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) outbreaks. They write “while the mortality rate for patients with SARS and MERS was around 10%, approximately half of the survivors experienced organ damage affecting their long-term health”.

The new definition was developed by a team of international experts in critical care, health services research, philosophy, bioethics, and epidemiology. The team was led by Dr. Shalini Mathur from the National University of Singapore (NUS) and Dr. Shamir Mehta from McMaster University in Canada. 

According to Dr. Mathur, “The current definition of critical illness has been around for over 50 years, and it’s time to change. Our proposed definition is more precise, and it better reflects the complex experience of patients and their families, especially in the era of COVID-19”.

Dr. Scott G. Frenchie, MD, FACP, CCPHQ, said, “We are trying to change the paradigm of how we staff ICU’s. ICU care is often provided by 2-3 critical care nurses and 1-2 doctors with specialty training in critical care. This model is often expensive and difficult to maintain, especially in rural communities. We are testing a new model that uses a primary care physician, 2 nurses, and a smart device that provides decision support to deliver the care. We are testing this in a rural community in Haiti. We will compare the quality of care and patient outcomes to traditional ICU care. If our hypothesis is correct, this could lead to more of a team approach to providing care in the ICU.”

Dr. Frenchie is a critical care and pulmonary physician, a PHQN certified health care quality professional, and an Associate Professor at the University of Texas Health Science Center.  He is the Founder and Director of the International Center for Health Professional Education and Research (ITCHER).  He has worked in Africa, Haiti, and the Middle East and has extensive experience in developing countries.  His passion is improving the quality of care delivered to the sickest of the sick.  He is married to a critical care and pulmonary physician and they often collaborate on projects.

They hope their work will lead to better outcomes for patients and their families, and a more standardized approach to defining and caring for critically ill patients.

Dr. Mitchell said: “We found that there is a wide variation in the definitions used. This makes it hard to compare studies and understand how many patients are critically ill at any given time. It also makes it hard to get a global sense of how many patients are placed on a breathing machine, the support they need for their blood pressure, or whether they need a kidney machine to filter their blood. Since these data are also used to plan for ICU capacity, understand staffing needs and plan for the supply of breathing machines and other equipment, these results are important for people planning for the future care of COVID patients.”

Dr. Kutsogiannis added: “Our study also found that most of the studies included in this review defined critical illness based on the use of breathing machines, which is a late sign of illness progression and does not capture the entire course of critical illness. This is an important finding because it suggests that we may be underestimating the total number of patients that are critically ill.”

Dr. Gardam concluded: “There are a number of reasons why the care of critically ill patients has not been well studied. Many of the patients who are very sick are in small rural hospitals that are not electronically connected to each other or to larger hospitals, so it is difficult to gather data from them. Many of the patients who are very sick are in intensive care units in large urban centres, but because of patient privacy reasons, it can be logistically difficult to gather data on them. This is an important study because it is the first to describe the landscape of critical illness in Canada, and it comes at a time when it is most needed.”

Abstract
Background The obligate intracellular parasite Plasmodium infects liver cells of mosquitoes and humans. Altered cytoskeletal organization is reported in parasite- and cytokine-induced liver cell transformation, however, the underlying molecular mechanisms are not known. Here, we used a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen to identify host factors important for altered microtubule organization during Plasmodium liver infection.
Results We identified 13 genes essential for malaria parasite development in liver cells. Of these genes, we validated four genes, CENPJ, PKNBY, DCTN1, and PCDH15, which were located in a region of chromosome 8 previously associated with malaria. CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of each gene resulted in altered microtubule organization, a key step in the establishment of malaria infection in the liver. We also observed altered lysosome morphology and accumulation of the autophagy marker protein LC3 (ATG8) on the surface of lysosomes in cells lacking CENPJ. Infection of cells with live Plasmodium parasites resulted in a dramatic reduction of the CENPJ protein and the microtubule-associated protein MAP2B in liver cells, indicating that both proteins are consumed for parasite development.
Conclusions Our genome-wide screen identified four novel host genes that are important for microtubule organization during malaria parasite infection. Furthermore, we identify the centrosome-associated protein CENPJ as a key regulator of autophagy and microtubule dynamics during host cell transformation and parasite infection.
Keywords:Malaria, Plasmodium, Liver, Autophagy, Microtubule, CENPJ, CRISPR-Cas9

At the initial stage of infection, liver-stage parasites (Ishikawa cells) localize to a microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a polarization pattern observed in both apicomplexan parasites and host cells infected with these parasites. Live-cell imaging of parasite-host co-cultures revealed that parasite movement was associated with dynamic microtubule plus-ends in the host cell. In the presence of the parasite, host microtubules were highly dynamic, with increased turnover and dramatic shifts in stability and polarity of microtubule ends, as revealed by live-cell imaging and western blot analyses of microtubule-associated proteins. We propose a model in which parasite motion is generated by the dynamic reorganization of host microtubules.

Microtubules are dynamic polymers of α/β-tubulin whose plus-ends are the sites of microtubule assembly and disassembly, a process regulated by a large number of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs).1,2 Microtubules are essential for a variety of cellular processes, including chromosome alignment during mitosis,3 body axis formation in Drosophila,4 and cilia function.5 In apicomplexan parasites, microtubules are essential for gliding motility,6,7 organelle transport,8 and possibly other processes, but the roles of microtubules in parasite-host interaction and in parasite cytoskeleton organization are less clear.

The microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a small body structure, serves as the main microtubule-organizing center in the eukaryotic cell, assembling and navigating microtubules in a polar and organized manner.9 In apicomplexan parasites, the MTOC is characterized as a small dot that organizes microtubules into a radial pattern,10 but the MTOC’s role in parasite microtubule organization and function is unknown. We present a model in which the host cell Golgi, a complex membrane bound organelle, is hijacked by the P. LS to establish a specialized organelle, the PVM, for which there is no known equivalent in host cells during normal conditions. This is the first time that the Golgi has been shown to be hijacked by an intracellular parasite to form a specialized organelle. Altogether, our data suggest a new model for how the P. LS forms a unique membrane-bound organelle for its survival in the host cell. We propose that the P. LS has co-opted the host cell secretory pathway to form the PVM and that this represents a new form of cellular piracy. This work has important implications for the field of apicomplexan biology since it provides a system for how a member of this ancient phylum co-opts a membrane bound organelle from the host cell to build a specialized parasitophorous vacuole. This work is also significant for the field of parasite biochemistry since it provides a new method for localizing proteins to this organelle.

However, the antiviral activity of these compounds was tested in Vero cells, which are susceptible to a wide range of animal viruses but not LS. Here, we present an LS-specific antiviral cell line (LuSi), which was used to test the antiviral activity of the four compounds in our study. LuSi cells were infected with LS at the same MOI as in our previous study. Four antiviral compounds were added at a 50 μM concentration, and the antiviral activity was measured by a cytopathic effect (CPE) assay at 96 h post-infection (hpi). IC50 values were calculated based on the dose-response curve at 96 hpi. All compounds inhibited LS infection in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 3a). The IC50 values of the four compounds in LuSi cells were 66.05, 58.48, 144.66, and 97.22 μM for PX-63, GRC-54208, GRC-59398, and GRC-61115, respectively (Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether the combination of two compounds had a stronger antiviral effect than each compound alone (Fig. 3c). The combination of PX-63 and GRC-54208 had the strongest synergistic effect, with an IC50 of 30.99 μM, followed by the combination of PX-63 and GRC-59398, with an IC50 of 17.52 μM. The combination of GRC-54208 and GRC-59398 had the lowest IC50 value (75.55 μM) of the three possible combinations we tested and showed a slightly additive effect. We next investigated whether the combination of one host-targeted compound and one lysosomal targeting compound had an additive effect on LS infection inhibition (Fig. 3d). The combination of PX-63 and CQ had an IC50 of 2.12 μM, followed by the combination of GRC-54208 and CQ, with an IC50 of 2.90 μM. The combination of PX-63 and LY-364,049 had the lowest IC50 value (2.05 μM) of the three possible combinations we tested and showed a slightly additive effect. These results suggest that the combination of host-targeted and lysosomal targeting compounds may have an additive effect on the inhibition of LS infection.

samples.src: Many parasites use the nutrients and resources of their human or animal host’s cells to reproduce themselves.

samples.hyp:
However, the parasites and their host cells have very different requirements for the types of cells in which they want to multiply. Host cells generally do not want to be taken over by parasites, and so the parasites need special mechanisms to evade the immune response of their host in order to survive. We still know relatively little about how parasites evade the immune response of their host. The human immune system uses special white blood cells called lymphocytes to eliminate parasites. These lymphocytes recognize parasites through parasite-specific proteins on the surface of these cells. These proteins are called major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I or II. The MHC presents short versions of parasite proteins to the lymphocytes as potential danger signals, which are then either attacked by the lymphocytes or ignored by the immune system. The parasite-specific proteins that are recognized by the lymphocytes are called restriction fragments (RFs). We still know relatively little about how the RFs of different parasites recognize the MHC of their host. We still know even less about how the RFs of different parasites recognize each other. In this project, we want to investigate how different parasites recognize each other through their RFs. We want to find out which RFs are present in different parasites and whether these RFs can be recognized by the human immune system. We will then use a special type of yeast to produce human MHC proteins and present the RFs of different parasites to the human immune system. This will allow us to find out which RFs are recognized by the human immune system and which RFs are not. This will allow us to create a catalog of RFs that can be used by the human immune system to recognize parasites. This catalog could then be used to program the human immune system to eliminate parasites that cause leprosy, sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, African river blindness, and Chagas disease. This would help to eliminate these harmful parasites from the human population. It would also help us to understand how parasites evade the immune response of their host and how they recognize each other.

The researchers used a new method to identify genes that are activated in the early stages of liver infection.

The researchers used human liver cells and lab tests to identify genes that are activated during the first stages of liver infection by the malaria parasite Plasmodium berghei. The researchers used a method called “multiomics” which combines genetic, protein, and cell biology information to identify genes that may play a role in specific biological processes. The method was used to identify genes that are activated during the interaction between the liver cells and the parasite.

The researchers found that the most significantly changed gene was a human gene called CXCL10. The researchers also identified a group of genes that are involved in the immune response of the liver to the parasite. The identified genes can be used to develop new diagnostic methods for malaria infection in humans, according to the researchers. The method can also be used to identify genes that are activated in other cell types during infections.

This is the first study that has used the multiomics approach to identify genes that are activated in the early stages of a liver infection, according to the researchers. The findings of the study provide new insights into the immune response of the liver to malaria infections, which could lead to new treatments or vaccines in the future.

However, the parasite is very clever and has developed resistance to the available antimalarial drugs. In the last 10 years, the number of approved antimalarial drugs has dropped from 10 to 2. These 2 drugs are now the only ones with a long enough half-life to reach the liver and kill the parasite before it can start infecting red blood cells. Unfortunately, both drugs have severe side effects and have the potential to cause severe health problems if taken over long periods of time. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new drugs that can be taken for a short period of time to clear the parasite and safely prevent relapse. This would allow the patient’s own immune system to clear the remaining parasites and help build up long-term immunity. 

The parasite spends a short period of its life cycle in red blood cells, causing the symptoms of malaria. If left untreated, the parasite releases merozoites which then infect new red blood cells. This results in the symptoms of malaria - fever, chills, vomiting and severe headaches. If the patient dies, the parasite is released into the environment where it mates, producing thousands of eggs which develop into male and female mosquitoes. The female mosquito transmits the parasite when it bites a new human host. 

The parasite has a complex life cycle, spending part of its time in red blood cells and the other part in the gut of the mosquito. The parasite in the mosquito’s gut must produce gametocytes, which are the sexual forms of the parasite. These form cells called gametocytes, which must develop into male and female forms ready to mate once the parasite is taken up in a mosquito bite. 

The parasite then spends a short period in the mosquito’s gut and is taken up in the mosquito’s saliva when it bites. At this point, the parasite must transform into an infective form called an sporozoite which travels to the mosquito’s salivary glands. 

Finally, upon entry into the body, Plasmodium heads straight for the liver to reproduce.

The most effective way to prevent malaria transmission is through vector control, which aims to reduce contact between people and mosquitoes by either killing or repelling the insects. The most widely used insecticidal intervention is treated mosquito nets (ITNs), which are estimated to have saved >700,000 lives between 2000 and 2015.1 However, these nets are only effective if they are properly cared for and used every night. ITN use is associated with several non-infectious adverse events, including injuries and deaths, which has led to low net use frequency and duration in some settings.2,3
Insecticide-treated items (ITIs) are a new intervention that combines the protective effect of ITNs with an attached device that releases an insecticidal vapour. The device is activated by the heat from a person’s body, which kills mosquitoes before they can bite.4 The use of ITIs has been shown to reduce all malaria transmission pathways, including the biting rate by mosquitoes, malaria sporozoite rates in mosquitoes, and Plasmodium falciparum infection rates in humans.5
The first-generation ITI is a net treated with insecticide and fitted with a small solar-powered vapourizer. When the device is worn on the head, it kills mosquitoes before they can transmit the malaria parasite.6 The second-generation ITI is a cylinder made of expanded polypropylene that can be filled with water. The Plasmodium falciparum chloroquine resistance transporter (PfCRT) is a key determinant of antimalarial drug resistance. However, its three-dimensional structure is still unknown. Here, we present the crystal structure of PfCRT in its drug binding conformation, determined to 3.35 Å resolution by cryo-electron microscopy. The structure reveals the binding site of drugs and confirms the high degree of variability in the binding pocket among different PfCRTs. The accessibility of the binding site suggests that PfCRT undergoes a conformational change upon drug binding. Our findings support a ‘jigsaw puzzle’ model for the development of drug resistance, in which multiple mutations are required for full resistance. The structure and dynamics of the drug binding site provide new information for further development of existing and future antimalarial drugs.

samples.src: Biological Invasions as a Component of South Africa’s Global Change Research Effort
samples.ref: Okulumbibwa kw’Ebitonde Ebigwira ng’omu ku Kaweefube wa South Afrika ow’Okukyusa Ensi okuyita mu Kunoonyereza
samples.hyp:
Global change encompasses a wide range of environmental and social changes, including climate change, changes in biodiversity, changes in human demographics and values, and changes in international political, economic, and social structures. Biological invasions are a common but often overlooked component of global change. Here, we assess the role of biological invasions in South Africa’s global change research effort. We show that biological invasions is a key component of South Africa’s long-term global change research effort, and that research in this area has increased significantly in recent years. We also show that biological invasions is a connected part of research into a wide range of other global change components, and that research in this area has strong links to social science global change research. Biological invasions is one of the major research themes in the South African National Biodiversity Institute, and a major component of the South African National Biodiversity Institute’s Long Term Ecological Research program. Biological invasions research in South Africa is also supported by a number of additional research grants and by at least one dedicated long-term research program. In view of the above, a national strategy for biological invasions research in South Africa is proposed.
