For each threat, we identified the most important ecosystem types most vulnerable to the threat, highlight knowledge gaps, and suggest research priorities.

We identified 216 articles relevant to our review. The most common ecosystem types threatened by multiple stressors included grasslands, rangelands, coastal areas, inland waters, and agricultural systems. Threats resulting in the most articles included biological invasions (39), habitat alteration and loss (30), climate change (29), overharvesting (21), and pollution (21). Estuaries were the most vulnerable coastal ecosystem to the threats evaluated, and grasslands were the most vulnerable inland ecosystem. Research priorities include the interactions, synergies, and trade-offs between stressors; the use of alternative approaches, such as new technology and economic models, to limit the impact of threats on ecosystems; and the need for management interventions to assist ecosystems in coping with and recovering from threats. Knowledge gaps include the effects of multiple stressors on ecosystems; degree and mechanisms of biological invasions, overharvesting, and pollution; drivers and consequences of habitat change; and the effects of climate change on species, communities, and ecosystems.

Results showed that the flow in the Mofolo catchment is highly interactive with base flow contributing an average of 46% of the total flow at the catchment outlet. In a new study, researchers surveyed and compared the number of publications in South Africa that cited invasive species as a threat to biodiversity conservation, between 1990 and 2019, with the number of publications that identified habitat change as the main threat. They found that both threats have been cited equally over the past three decades, in line with global findings. The study is the first to look at the temporal trend of the two threats in the context of research output in South Africa.
Invasive species are non-native organisms that have been introduced to an area where they did not naturally occur, and spread rapidly, out-competing and replacing native species and altering ecological dynamics. They have been shown to have far-reaching effects on the structure and function of ecosystems, as well as on human health and food security. Invasive species are listed as one of the key direct drivers of biodiversity loss in the IPBES Global Assessment Report, and in South Africa’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP), which identifies them as the second-largest threat to biodiversity, after habitat change.
To find out how much research attention invasive species receive in South Africa, compared to habitat change as a threat to biodiversity, the researchers - from the South African Environmental Observation Network (SAEON) and the University of KwaZulu-Natal (UKZN) - looked at two scoping bibliometric studies that have been done to date. One of these studies considered all publications that cited invasive species as a threat to biodiversity conservation between 1900 and 2018. The other considered all publications that identified habitat change as the main threat to biodiversity between 1950 and 2018. The current study combined these two datasets and considered the period 1990–2019, which is when most of the publications identified habitat change as the main threat.
The team found that invasive species have been cited as the second-largest threat since 2000, which is when most of the publications that identified habitat change as the main threat were published. The number of publications that identified habitat change as the main threat has been declining since 2010. In this context, we used a comprehensive and consistent assessment of global change drivers in 10 study regions to develop a first quantitative, multi-scale picture of their relative importance. Our results indicate that regions show distinct patterns in the relative importance of drivers, with pronounced differences at both the regional and local scale. In the Po Valley, Italy, land use is the most important driver at all scales, mainly due to its strong impact on soil properties. In the Great Plains, USA, land use and climate are of similar importance, with local patterns largely driven by the strong spatial heterogeneity in climate. In the Cerrado, Brazil, climate is the most important driver at all scales, and in the headwater catchments of the Luangwa River, Zambia, land use and climate are of similar importance. Our results demonstrate that an assessment of global change drivers at multiple scales provides a more comprehensive picture of the relative importance of drivers than a focus at a single scale. To move forward, we suggest that (1) more comprehensive studies are needed that combine biophysical and socio-economic research at different scales and (2) more attention should be paid to cross-scale interactions, which are often not considered in driver studies. Our approach can be used to develop a consistent assessment of global change drivers across different regions, and can be applied to other study regions to gain insight into the relative importance of drivers at different spatial scales.

A team of researchers from the University of Cape Town (UCT) and the University of KwaZulu-Natal (UKZN) has received R2.7 million to study the combined effects of climate change, invasive species and human activities on vegetation in South Africa.

The three-year study, led by UCT’s Associate Professor Ryan Pearson and UKZN’s Professor Richard Bradshaw, will look at how climate change, invasive species and changes in human activities are likely to affect the vegetation of South Africa’s diverse landscapes.

The project, “Vegetation mapping and modelling of the combined effects of climate change, invasive species and human activities in South Africa”, has been funded by the National Research Foundation (NRF) and the South African Department of Science and Innovation (DSI).

The researchers will use the funding to develop new species distribution models that incorporate multiple human activities and the effects of invasive species on vegetation. These models will build on existing climate models, which show how climate change is likely to affect the distribution of vegetation across South Africa’s diverse landscapes.

Invasive species are defined as non-native species that have established populations and are known to spread. The species most likely to be included in the study include alien trees and shrubs, as well as acacias, which are native to North Africa and Australia but are now widespread in South Africa.

“This project is important because it will help us understand how multiple drivers are likely to affect vegetation in South Africa, and how this may feedback into human activities,” Pearson said.

The project will also train postgraduate students to work with the novel species distribution models that will be developed during the project.

“Understanding and being able to predict how vegetation will respond to these multiple changes is crucial to being able to maintain ecosystem services such as clean water and food production into the future,” Pearson said.

In a paper published in the journal Diversity and Distributions, the team presents a bibliography of invasive species in South Africa. 

The team’s aim is to give an overview of the knowledge produced to date in this field and to highlight gaps in our understanding of invasive species in South Africa.

They found 262 publications on invasive species between 1990 and 2019. 

“While invasive species are the second greatest threat to biodiversity in South Africa, surprisingly only 262 papers have been published in the last 30 years, which is fewer than for some other threats such as climate change,” says Dr. Veena Venkataraman, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pretoria.

The team’s bibliography will be a living document that they will update periodically. “We hope that it will be a useful resource for scientists, managers, policy makers as well as the broader public, to reference and cite in future works and publications on invasive species in South Africa,” says Dr. Venkataraman.

The team is now working on a model to prioritise the control of invasive species based on the degree of threat they pose to biodiversity. 

“We aim to make decisions based on scientific evidence, and to do that we need a better understanding of where and to what extent these species have invaded, what areas have been lost, and which species are currently impacting our biodiversity the most,” says Dr. Venkataraman.

The team is also working on a model that combines all invasive species information into a single map to improve spatial prioritisation for management and conservation planning.

samples.hyp:
However, SOM is also highly vulnerable to disturbances such as fire, windthrow, and harvesting. In this study, we investigated how different harvest intensities affect SOM dynamics and its associated processes in two boreal forests of different composition in eastern Canada. Harvesting intensities were (1) no harvesting (control), (2) commercial thinning where 40% of the basal area was removed, and (3) clearcutting with different residual trees (25, 50, and 100 trees ha−1). We used a direct sampling approach and measured in situ SOM fluxes associated with root exudation and microbial respiration as well as SOM stocks. Microbial respiration was also measured in incubations without root exudation. Harvesting significantly reduced SOM stocks, especially for the O horizon, and the effect was more pronounced in the clearcutting treatment. In the O horizon, SOM stocks three years after treatment ended were 25–30% of the control for clearcutting with 25 and 50 trees ha−1, but were still 56% of the control for commercial thinning and clearcutting with 100 trees ha−1. Net nitrification rates were significantly increased in the mineral soil by clearcutting and by commercial thinning, especially with higher residual trees. In the O horizon, net nitrification rates were also significantly increased by clearcutting, but we did not detect any treatment effect on microbial respiration or SOM fluxes. Harvesting had a greater impact on SOM stocks in the conifer forest (−36%) than in the mixedwood forest (−16%), probably because of the difference in harvesting intensity and in site productivity. Our results suggest that the intensity of harvesting and the residual tree retention affect SOM stocks and processes in boreal forests, but in different ways for the O and mineral soil.

Here we assess variability in SOM and C stocks in response to edaphic, biotic and fire variables at the landscape-scale in a miombo woodland in South Africa. Soils were sampled across a gradient of clay content (0–40%), along a topographic gradient (low, mid and high) and fire frequency categories (>1, 2–4 and >5 years). Soil samples were analyzed for organic C, total N, clay content and pH. Stocks of organic C in the top 20 cm of soil were estimated. Results showed that clay content was the predominant factor influencing SOM and C stocks. Topography and fire frequency had no influence on SOM or C stocks. The influence of clay content on SOM and C stocks was most pronounced at the lowest clay content sites. At these sites, SOM and C stocks were 84.1 and 54.1 Mg ha−1, respectively, for sites with 0–7% clay content compared to 210.0 and 136.2 Mg ha−1, respectively, for sites with 30–40% clay content. Mean organic C stocks were 2.3-fold and 2.7-fold greater at high and medium clay content sites, respectively, compared to low clay content sites. Our results show that variability in clay content is an important factor influencing SOM and C stocks in miombo woodlands which needs to be considered in carbon accounting for these ecosystems.

Posted by Richard Ahern - 23/01/2023 07:00 AM

# Cut trees carefully to improve soil, say scientists studying Zambian forests

Scientists have found that cutting trees can actually improve the soil quality in Zambia's forests, but only if it is done carefully.

The study, conducted by researchers from the University of Central Florida, found that the soil in Zambian forests that had been recently logged had higher levels of carbon and nutrients than undisturbed forests.

This is because when trees are cut, the stump and roots are left in the ground, which helps to break up the soil and allow for better drainage. This, in turn, can help to reduce erosion and improve the overall health of the forest.

However, if the trees are not cut carefully, the soil can be severely damaged. When the trunks are left on the ground, they can prevent rainwater from reaching the soil, leading to drought conditions. Additionally, the stumps can make it difficult for new trees to grow, as they take up valuable space and resources.

To ensure that tree cutting does more good than harm, the researchers suggest harvesting only a portion of the trees in a given area, and carefully removing the stumps and roots after cutting. They also advise using the harvested wood for sustainable purposes, such as building materials or fuel.

While tree cutting can be a necessary practice in some cases, such as to create space for farming or to reduce the risk of forest fires, it is important to do so in a way that minimizes the negative impacts on the environment.

In conclusion, while tree cutting can have negative effects on the environment, it is possible to do so in a way that actually improves the soil quality. By carefully harvesting trees and removing the stumps and roots, we can help to create healthier forests that can better support the wildlife and people who depend on them.

Keywords: tree cutting, soil quality, zambian forests, university of central florida, carbon, nutrients, erosion, overall health, drought conditions, building materials, fuel, forest fires, wildlife, people.

However, soil quality is a complex concept that is hard to measure. In this article, we propose a simple method to assess soil quality. Our method is based on the principle that healthy soils are able to support primary production (crop and tree yield), are able to function as a habitat for soil organisms, and are able to maintain these functions in the face of external challenges like drought. We apply this method to a large dataset (2223 soil and crop yield observations) from farmers in Malawi to show how soil quality changes along soil properties like soil texture and nutrients, and how these relationships change along agro-ecological zones. We also show how soil quality changes after the introduction of conservation agriculture (CA) practices. Our results show that soil quality is indeed related to soil properties and crop yield, and that soil properties have a bigger impact on soil quality than crop yield. We also find that soil quality is higher in the central and southern parts of Malawi, compared to the northern parts. Our results also show that CA has a positive effect on soil quality. Together, these results suggest that while crop yield is an important factor of soil quality, soil properties and management practices have an even bigger impact on soil quality. Therefore, to improve soil quality, it is important to focus not only on crop yields but also on soil properties and management practices.

This article presents a method to assess soil quality in subsistence farming systems in Malawi and explores how this soil quality changes along soil properties and agro-ecological zones, and how it responds to the implementation of CA practices.

Most of the soil carbon in these soils is found in the top 20 cm, so this depth is usually chosen for sampling. 

But a new study, published recently in Agronomy Journal, shows that the depth at which samples are collected can influence the results. 

The study was conducted by Hugues Mambo, a soil scientist with the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), and his colleagues. The aim was to determine the effect of different sampling depths on carbon and organic matter determination in two types of soils, one low in organic matter and the other high in organic matter. 

The study was conducted at IITA’s grounds in Ibadan, Nigeria. Soil samples were collected in 20-cm deep sub-samples from two main layers: 0-20 cm (the conventional sampling depth) and 20-40 cm. The samples were analyzed for organic matter, total nitrogen (N), microbial biomass carbon (MBC), and potentially mineralizable N. 

The results showed that the two different depths gave different results. The 0-20 cm samples had on average 1.84% organic matter and 0.28% total N. The 20-40 cm samples had significantly (10%) higher organic matter (2.05%) but significantly (10%) lower total N (0.24%). This was not surprising to the researchers because the top 20 cm of soil is generally more fertile, being the layer where most plant roots and microorganisms are found. 

The researchers also used the results to calculate carbon sequestration rates, finding that the 20-40 cm layer could store 1.5 tons more carbon per hectare per year than the 0-20 cm layer. This means that if samples are collected from just the 0-20 cm layer, carbon sequestration rates will be underestimated by 0.5 ton per hectare per year. 

The researchers concluded that sampling depth is an important factor that can affect soil organic carbon measurements. They recommended that future studies should collect samples from both the 0-20 cm and the 20-40 cm layers in order to get a complete picture of what is happening in the soil.

The researchers used statistical models to calculate where in Africa COVID-19 infections were the most prevalent, and how quickly the virus spread in different parts of the continent. They found that the number of cases in each country or territory was a good indicator of how fast the virus spread there, and that the timing of the first reported cases was a good indicator of the actual start of the epidemic. The researchers also looked at how the epidemic was managed in each country or territory. They found that the epidemic was slower in countries or territories that took more aggressive control measures, such as border closures and movement restrictions. The researchers say the models they developed could be used to plan for potential future epidemics and help guide public health policies to slow down the spread of infectious diseases. They also suggest that the models could be used to test how effective different control measures are. "By continuously running these models with the latest data, public health officials can make rapid decisions that determine how severe a potential epidemic might be and how best to mitigate its effects," says Kadau. "This is important for African countries, which generally have fewer resources to handle a large number of cases." The researchers are now working to validate their models against other data sets, and they hope to partner with other teams to further develop the models. "We are also looking into how we can implement these models to support public health officials in their daily operations," says Kadau. More information: Jacob R. The study was published in the open access journal IAFOR.

Forests are a vital part of our ecosystem, and they play a crucial role in the global water cycle, climate, and biodiversity. However, forests are under pressure from many front: forest loss, degradation, fragmentation, and climate change. The need for sustainable forest management is acute, and we need to ensure that our forests will be around for future generations.

The Congo Basin is one of the largest forest regions in the world, and it is also one of the most threatened. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that between 1990 and 2010, the area of forest in the Congo Basin declined by 5.3 million hectares, an area larger than Denmark. This rate of loss is slightly lower than the global average, but the Basin is located in a biodiversity hotspot, and there is a high pressure on the forest resources. In response, the Central African Forest Initiative (CAFI) was launched in 2008 by the government of the Republic of Congo, the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the government of Gabon. CAFI is a public-private partnership that supports sustainable management of the forest resources while contributing to the countries’ socio-economic development.

To help monitor the implementation of CAFI, an international team of researchers from the University of Antwerp (Belgium), the University of Copenhagen (Denmark), and the Wildlife Conservation Society (United States) studied dynamics of forest cover change in the Congo Basin, using annual time series of Landsat satellite images, collected between 1990 and 2020.

The study revealed that forest loss and degradation are concentrated in the eastern part of the Congo Basin, and that the rate of loss is increasing. The researchers also found that the most common cause of forest loss was selective logging. “Our study shows that the forest cover change in the Congo Basin is not homogeneous, with the eastern part being the most dynamic and the southern part the most stable,” said Dr. Philippe Mokonda, a researcher at the University of Antwerp and lead author of the study. “This in-depth knowledge of the drivers and rates of forest cover change is essential to effectively design and implement forest management strategies and actions,” he added.

The protein in chickpeas is of high biological value because it contains all the essential amino acids required by humans. The oil in chickpeas is rich in unsaturated fatty acid which is good for human health. Ethiopia produces about 2.8 million tons of chickpeas per year. However, the production is characterized by yield gap between the research obtained yield and the farmers’ yield. The yield gap is high, and it is about 3.0 t/ha. The major constraints of chickpea production in Ethiopia are biotic and abiotic factors. The major biotic constraints are disease, insects and weeds while the major abiotic ones are iron deficiency, salinity, drought and sub-optimum temperature. Chickpea is a self-pollinating crop and it is cross-pollinated by insects mostly by bees and less by flies and beetles. The crop is mainly outcrossed when it is grown in the areas where there are two or more cultivars. The amount of cross-pollination depends on the abundance of pollinators, floral architecture, and the distance between two plants. The proportion of outcrossed plants was reported to be from 14 to 100%. In Ethiopia, there is a lack of information on the amount of cross-pollination and its effect on the yield and yield components. Therefore, the objective of this study was to assess the degree of cross-pollination and its effect on yield and yield components in selected chickpea cultivars in Ethiopia. Ten chickpea cultivars were used in this study. The cultivars were selected based on their popularity in Tigray, Amhara, Afar, and Oromia regions of Ethiopia. The Platform is co-ordinated by the International Center for Chickpea and Mungbean (ICCM), a CGIAR Research Program on Dryland Cereals (DRY), in collaboration with the National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS) of India, Australia, Turkey and France, and the private sector. The Platform was established in the framework of the CERN (Genome) and the associated technologies were developed in the framework of the Australian Research Council Linkage Project: “Genomic selection in lentil and chickpea: a efficiency breeding tool for producers in low and medium input systems” (LP110100627), in collaboration with the International Center for Inland Valley Salmonids (ICIVS), the International Center for Chickpea and Mungbean (ICCM) and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT).

The Platform aims to:

  • Improve understanding of the chickpea market and value chain to better target research and development investments;
  • Identify research and development needs and priorities and ensure that such improvements are want-based and demand-driven;
  • Promote and facilitate adoption of research results and technology by public and private organizations, and by farmers;
  • Enhance collaboration and coordination among researchers, development agents and public and private organizations involved in the improved technologies; and
  • Improve research prioritization in NARS/CGIAR/FAO programs in order to maximize synergies among all stakeholders and to maximize the impact of research on poverty alleviation and food and nutrition security.

The Platform is a CGIAR Strategic Research and Scientific Innovation (SRSI) Platform and is recognized by the CGIAR’s Executive Board. The Platform is open to a variety of organizations and stakeholders involved in the chickpea research-for-development chain, and in particular to organizations and stakeholders in developing countries. The Platform is co-chaired by the ICCM Director and the Director of the Indian Institute of Crop Science (IICRS), and the Platform’s Management Committee includes representatives from Australia, France, India, and Turkey. The Platform is currently being formalized through the establishment of a legal entity in India. The Platform’s activities are supported by the ICCM and by the Australian Research Council through the National Chickpea Research Program project: “Chickpea breeding and pre-breeding enhancement using genetic mapping, association mapping, and marker-assisted selection with focus on abiotic stresses” (LP120100533).

In the case of the orange sweet potato, the platform brought together scientists, plant breeders, agricultural extension workers, and farmers in a collaborative effort to promote the new variety. The platform used a multi-pronged strategy to promote the new orange variety, including providing training and technical support to extension workers, encouraging the use of print and broadcast media, and establishing a presence at major agricultural events. These efforts led to a nearly tenfold increase in the number of farmers planting the orange variety (from 30,000 in 2003 to 300,000 in 2005). The platform also helped to diffuse other improved varieties of sweet potato, including one with resistance to sweet potato fever, which affects storage roots, and a purple-fleshed variety that is high in antioxidants.

The platform approach was so successful that it was replicated with other crops, including banana, maize, and wheat. In the case of banana, the platform brought together plant breeders and extension workers to design a strategy to diffuse a new heat-tolerant, high-yielding, and drought-resistant variety developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in Ibadan. The new variety, known as “GISAN-1,” is the first of its kind in the world that is both disease resistant and high yielding. From May through July 2010, the platform conducted a “test launch” in five sites in Uganda to further refine its strategies for diffusing the new variety. The test involved a range of activities, including field days, radio images, and community screening. The launch of the banana variety is scheduled for early 2011.

The platform also helped to promote a new variety of maize developed by IITA to be resistant to the major pests in Africa, including the maize stalk borer, which can cause economic losses in excess of 80 percent in some areas. A test launch of this variety was conducted in Uganda and Tanzania during August and September 2010. The launch is scheduled for January 2011. Chickpeas are an important crop for millions of farmers in Ethiopia, where production is highly variable due to drought, disease and pests. But production has more than doubled over the last six years, reaching 32 000 tonnes in 2020, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Exports have also increased, thanks to support from the African Development Bank, which has helped Ethiopia improve the quality and value addition of the crop.

The Bank has been important in helping Ethiopia achieve its goal of becoming a net food-exporting country by 2025. The Bank is one of the leading contributors to the country’s economic development through the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP), which has contributed to improved food security and resilience in Ethiopia.

The Bank has supported the country’s agriculture sector policy and strategic roadmap, which aims to double agriculture productivity and achieve 100 percent agricultural income growth by 2025. The Bank is also financing agriculture development projects in Ethiopia, including the recently launched Ethiopia Sustainable Agricultural Land Management Project, which aims to enhance the resilience of smallholder farmers to climate change through the sustainable management of agricultural land.

The increase in chickpea production can be attributed to a number of factors. These include the right type of variety, good agronomic practices, integrated crop management, and the use of good quality seed.

The increase in production can also be attributed to the establishment of farmer field schools, which have helped farmers identify problems and find solutions to overcome production constraints. The establishment of chickpea processing industries has also played a major role in increasing production.

samples.src: Researchers report on SARS-CoV-2 variant evolution in Uganda
samples.ref: Abanoonyereza balina bye bagamba ku kika kya SARS-CoV-2 mu Uganda
samples.hyp:
A new preprint paper* reports that, based on analysis of 349 whole genome sequences of SARS-CoV-2 from Uganda, a new variant of the virus has emerged. The researchers also note a shift in the proportion of genomic mutations in this dataset, with 3.6% of the sequences now containing mutations that were absent or less prevalent in earlier samples. The most prevalent mutations in the new variant include E484K in the spike protein, which has been associated with immune evasion, and N501Y in the receptor-binding domain of the spike protein, which has been reported to increase binding of the virus to the human receptor.

The authors note that the proportion of sequences containing the E484K mutation, observed in 1.4% of the whole genome sequences and 24.1% of the spike protein sequences, is of concern because this mutation has been linked to escape from neutralizing antibodies in multiple studies and because it is part of the same spike protein mutation cluster that has been associated with the B.1.351 (South Africa) and P.1 (Brazil) variants.

The researchers also examined whether there were differences in transmissibility, disease severity, or vaccine efficacy associated with the new variant. They found that individuals who tested positive for the variant were less likely to be symptomatic (52%) compared to individuals who tested positive for other variants (62%), and they also found that the new variant was significantly less likely to be hospitalised or die compared to other variants. However, given that these were unvaccinated individuals, the authors also note that it is possible that being unvaccinated rather than the specific viral variant led to these differences in health outcomes.

The authors write that “Given the importance of spike protein amino acid composition in immune recognition and vaccine efficacy, the frequent occurrence of the B.1.1.54 spike mutations and their potential impact on vaccine recognition should be of concern.”

The study didn’t find any differences in vaccine recognition between the new variant and other variants, but the authors write that “further analysis of vaccine evasion by B.1.1.54 is required given the concerning spike mutations observed in this variant.”

The authors conclude that “ongoing genomic surveillance for detection of variants of concern is essential to guide public health policies and interventions.”

The paper is available here and a press release from the University of Kent is available here.

*J. Sabin et al. Emergence, transmission and vaccine evasion of the SARS-CoV-2 B.1.1.

Uganda has to date recorded 96,265 COVID-19 cases and 2,608 deaths. The country has been recording between 100 and 150 new cases daily over the last week, with a total of 4,218 cases reported in the last seven days, according to the Ministry of Health.

The B.1.1.7 variant, which was first identified in UK, has so far been detected in 36 samples, of which three are from December 2020 while the rest are from the last few months. It has been detected in Kampala (20 samples), Northern (9), Eastern (4), Western (2), and Central (1) regions, the researchers noted.

The B.1.351 variant, first detected in South Africa, has been detected in six Ugandan samples, all of which were from January and February this year. It has been recorded in Eastern (2) and Western (4) Uganda, according to the study.

The P.1 variant, first detected in Brazil, has thus far only been detected in one sample, which was from Kampala. However, given that travel from and to Brazil has been very common, other infections might have occurred, the researchers said.

The researchers said the high number of untyped variants call for more surveillance and research to detect and characterise new variants.

“We show how rapid adaptation to new conditions can be achieved by the virus without the need for large mutations in the genome,” study coauthor Raul Ribeiro, a computational biologist at the University Hospital Center in Lausanne, Switzerland, said in a statement. “This is good news because it means that the virus may have a limited number of paths to evade our immune response and the vaccines we develop.”

To track the evolution of SARS-CoV-2, Ribeiro and his colleagues sequenced the viral genomes of 79 people in Switzerland who had been hospitalized for COVID-19. The team focused on the spike protein, which the virus uses to enter cells; the researchers compared how the protein varied between individuals and over time within individuals.

The researchers used statistical models to calculate where in Africa COVID-19 infections were the most prevalent, and how quickly the virus spread in different parts of the continent.

The models suggest the first wave of infections in Switzerland came mainly from Europe, while later waves were driven by variants that emerged in Africa. A more infectious variant from South Africa also contributed to the infections in Switzerland, the team reports. Although the variant had a higher reproduction number—a measure of how many people an infected person can transmit the virus to—than the variants already circulating in Switzerland, the authors note, the variant accounted for only a small fraction of cases.

Importantly, the researchers did not find any mutations in the spike protein that would make vaccines less effective. “Our analysis suggests that the vaccines currently being used in Switzerland will still be able to deal with these new variants,” Ribeiro said.

“It’s great that they’re looking at the post-vaccination period because we need to understand how durable the immunity is,” said Dr. David Gevers, an evolutionary geneticist at Ghent University in Belgium, who wasn’t involved in the study. “It’s good news if [the study] says that the vaccines are able to deal with the variants, but we should not be surprised if there are escapes, even though it may take some time.”

The prevalence of female genital mutilation (FGM) is highest in Africa, where 92 million women and girls have undergone FGM. FGM is most common in Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Sudan, and Uganda. Female genital cutting/mutilation is also practiced in other parts of the world, including North America and Australia. Female genital cutting/mutilation is nearly always carried out on minors, with girls usually cut between the ages of 4 and 15. The procedure often involves removal of the clitoris and sometimes the labia minora. Female genital cutting/mutilation can result in severe bleeding, infection, and psychological trauma. In some cases, girls have died from FGM. Female genital cutting/mutilation also increases the risk of complications in childbirth. Female genital cutting/mutilation is considered a violation of human rights by the United Nations and other international organizations. The United Nations has launched a campaign to eliminate female genital cutting/mutilation by 2030. In addition to the health risks, female genital cutting/mutilation also has cultural and social dimensions. The practice is often seen as a necessary part of a girl’s transition to womanhood. However, there is no medical justification for female genital cutting/mutilation. Female genital cutting/mutilation is a harmful practice that can have serious long-term health consequences. All girls and women have a right to safe, respectful care of their bodies. We need to do more to raise awareness of the harm caused by female genital cutting/mutilation and to support efforts to eliminate this practice.

For example, responses to items regarding research benefits were coded into four categories: 1) no awareness of any benefits, 2) mention of direct material benefits to themselves or others, 3) mention of broader community benefits and 4) other. This provided an indication of the frequency of different types of response to each open-ended item. In phase one, a training programme was conducted in 36 primary health care centres in Somalia, and 36 health workers were trained to communicate effectively with girls and women about FGM/C, and to provide them with information about the consequences of FGM/C. The training programme was developed by UNICEF Somalia in collaboration with the Somali Ministry of Health and partners, and drew on the ‘6 Cs framework for communication in health’ and social cognitive theory. Trainers were identified from among the health workers themselves, and conducted the training in their own facilities. The training included group discussions, role-play, and verbal and written tests. Health workers who received the training were compared with 36 untrained health workers in terms of their communication with girls and women, and the impact of training on girls’ and women’s decisions about FGM/C was assessed 12 months after training.

A total of 479 girls and women who had undergone FGM/C and 340 girls and women who had not, were surveyed. Qualitative analysis of focus group discussions with girls and women revealed that health workers were often seen as credible sources of information and advice about FGM/C. Quantitative analysis showed that health workers who received training made more suggestions for the future (e.g. ‘leave school to finish later’) and suggested FGM/C-related negative consequences that were more severe (e.g. ‘pain during childbirth’), compared to untrained health workers. Girls who had not undergone FGM/C were more likely to have undergone FGM/C if they trusted their health worker and if their health worker had suggested less severe consequences. Girls’ and women’s decisions about FGM/C were also more likely to be in line with social norms if they trusted their health worker and if their health worker had suggested less severe consequences.

This study provides some of the first evidence of the impact of health worker communication about FGM/C in Somalia. Health worker communication with girls and women about FGM/C may help to delay the age at which girls undergo FGM/C. There is a need to further explore the role of parents in decision-making. Parents are often overlooked as key stakeholders in the health and well-being of children with chronic conditions. This study aimed to explore and describe the decision-making process of parents of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). A qualitative, descriptive study was conducted based on data collected from 18 parents of children with JIA. Individual interviews, participant-observation in a JIA clinic, and document analysis were performed. Data were analyzed using an inductive approach. Parents shared that they are involved in all dimensions of decision-making, including preparation, shared decision-making, and implementation. However, parents expressed that they are often unprepared for the decision-making process and may make decisions based on emotions. They also described the challenges of balancing the desire for involvement with clinical expertise. Parents may be empowered through increased education and support to make empowered decisions for their children.

To stop female genital mutilation, we first need to understand why it’s happening

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines female genital mutilation (FGM) as any procedure that involves altering or injuring the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. This practice has been widely performed in 29 African countries and in the Middle East, where around 80% of girls and women have undergone FGM. The practice has also been performed in Asia and Latin America, but to a lesser extent.

Female genital mutilation is often performed on girls under the age of 5, and sometimes on infants as young as 3 days old. In some places, the procedure is performed in one session, while in others it is done in several sessions over a few years. In the most severe forms of FGM, the girl’s genitals are completely removed.

The practice of female genital mutilation is a complex issue with deep roots in tradition, religion, and social norms. It is important to understand the reasons behind this practice in order to develop effective interventions to stop it.

Cultural and social factors

Female genital mutilation is often seen as a cultural tradition that is passed down from one generation to the next. In some communities, it is believed that FGM is necessary to prepare a girl for womanhood, marriage, and childbearing. It is also seen as a way to ensure a girl’s purity and to control her sexuality.

However, it is important to note that FGM is not supported by any religion or culture. In fact, the practice is increasingly being recognized as a human rights violation and a form of violence against women and girls.

Psychological factors

Female genital mutilation is often performed for cultural or social reasons, but it can also be a result of psychological factors. In some cases, parents or caregivers may subject their daughters to FGM in an attempt to control their sexuality or to punish them for perceived misbehavior.

It is important to note that FGM is not a necessary or appropriate response to concerns about a girl’s sexuality or behavior. There are many ways to address these issues without resorting to harmful practices like FGM.

Economic factors

In some cases, female genital mutilation may be performed for economic reasons. In areas where the practice is common, families may feel pressure to have their daughters undergo FGM in order to be considered eligible for marriage. This can create a cycle of poverty, as families may spend a significant amount of money on the procedure and related expenses, such as travel to a practitioner.

The researchers asked them about their experiences of being cut, and about the consequences of the procedure. They also asked the young women what they thought about FGM, and why they thought it was carried out. The young women’s responses were very similar to those given by older women who had undergone FGM. The researchers also found that FGM had affected these young people’s relationships, and had prevented them from engaging in daily activities. The young women were also afraid that they would be cut in the future. Many of them knew of other young women who had been cut. Some of them had been threatened with being cut again if they did not keep silent about the fact that they had suffered FGM. This showed the difficulties that even young women who had suffered FGM faced.
The researchers wrote: ‘These findings suggest that FGM is more than just a health issue. It is a social issue that has been passed from one generation to another, and it affects not only the women who undergo it, but also those who have not. It is time for the social factors that influence FGM to be addressed.’
The researchers concluded that health education campaigns were important, but that more needed to be done. They wrote: ‘Other strategies, such as those that aim to address the social factors that influence FGM, need to be implemented in order to have a more sustainable and comprehensive effect on FGM.’
This research was published in the journal BMC International Health and Human Rights.

The study was conducted in the Sidama zone of the Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples Region in Ethiopia. This region was selected, because FGM is very common there. The ‘Yes I Do’ programme is implemented by the World Health Organization (WHO), the Minister of Health of the Netherlands and the Dutch organization SNV.

The aim of the study was to gain more insight into the beliefs, attitudes and practices regarding FGM and to identify the main actors and their networks that are involved in FGM, in order to strengthen the ‘Yes I Do’ programme. The study used both quantitative and qualitative methods. Questionnaires were given to 1,200 women (600 in the intervention group and 600 in the control group). In addition, 100 in-depth interviews were conducted and 30 key informant interviews were done. Furthermore, four focus group discussions with 80 women were organized.

The study showed that the Sidama have their own long tradition with the initiation of girls (‘niw’ele’) which is not considered as FGM, but more like a rite of passage. The ‘niw’ele’ ceremony is performed at the beginning of adolescence and consists of four main steps. First, the hair on the girl’s pubic region is shaved. Second, the girl is given a traditional Sidama dress. Third, the girl is initiated in the Sidama traditional values. Fourth, the girl is given a Sidama name. The ‘niw’ele’ ceremony is performed by the village midwife or health extension worker. The ‘niw’ele’ ceremony is not considered a sign of belonging to a certain group, does not involve bloodshed and is not painful. In the Sidama culture, it is not seen as a problem if a girl has not been through the ‘niw’ele’ ceremony. Therefore, the Sidama do not see themselves as performing FGM. This explains why FGM is hard to eradicate in the Sidama region.

samples.src: Reproductive Hormones Imbalance, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Ultrastructural Changes in Testis of African Giant Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Intoxication
samples.ref: Obunafu bwa Homoni enzaazi, okufa kw’akataffaali akayitibwa Germ Cell Apoptosis, Enkwaso Eziriko Obulemu n’Enkyukakyuka mu Kikula ky’Ensigo z’emmese ensolima (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) nga zikubiddwa ekirungo kya Sodium Metavanadate
samples.hyp:
The effects of sodium metavanadate (NaMO) on the male reproductive system of African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus) were investigated. Animals were divided into four groups and treated as follows: group I served as control; group II was administered NaMO at a single dose of 2.5 mg/kg body weight; group III received NaMO at a single dose of 5 mg/kg body weight; and group IV was administered NaMO at an accumulative dose of 2.5 mg/kg body weight for four consecutive days. Testicular relative weights, tail lengths of sperm, and sperm parameters were significantly (p < 0.05) decreased in all treated groups compared to the control. Apoptotic cells were detected in the testes of rats treated with NaMO, and the apoptosis rate was significantly increased in a dose-dependent manner. The principal piece and annular crests were fused together in some spermatozoa, and the fibrous sheath was partially disorganized in the treated groups. These results suggest that NaMO-induced testicular damage is related to the disruption of the structural integrity of the sperm flagella and apoptotic changes in the testicular tissues, which could be due to reproductive hormone imbalance.

The following glossary is provided for this text:

Glossary:
annular crest: a dense ring of microtubules located at the base of the middle piece.
apoptosis: a type of cell death that occurs in multicellular organisms.
cell: the smallest unit of an organism that can carry on the essential life processes of that organism.
flagellum: tail-like structure found on certain cells, especially sperm, that enables motion.
germ cell: a cell that is the precursor of a gamete, especially a male gamete.
middle piece: region of a spermatozoon between the head and the tail that is filled with mitochondria.
spermatozoon: a motile and metabolically active cell that, in most species, is responsible for delivering sperm to the female in order to fertilize it.
ultrastructure: the internal structure of a cell or other small cell-like structure as revealed by an electron microscope.

samples.src: Researchers say metal found in polluted air makes rats infertile
samples.ref: Abanoonyereza bagamba nti obuuma obusangibwa mu mpewo eyonooneddwa egumbawaza emmese
samples.hyp:
Published: 01 April 2010 (modified: 06 April 2010) (viewed: 483 times)

Author: Nicky Webb

Rats exposed to metal particles found in polluted air become infertile, researchers have found.

The study, by scientists at the University of Edinburgh, could explain why human fertility is falling in some parts of the world.

The researchers exposed female rats to high levels of iron-rich particles similar to those found in urban air. The animals became infertile and their reproductive organs showed signs of inflammation.

The study, which was funded by the Medical Research Council and Natural Environment Research Council, also showed that the effects could be passed on to future generations.

The researchers say the findings suggest that pollution may be having a more significant impact on fertility than previously thought.

The study has been published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA.


Professor Bill Charles, of the University of Edinburgh’s School of Biological Sciences, said: “We found that when females are exposed to particulate matter, they are more likely to suffer from inflammation of the reproductive organs, and pass it on to their offspring. This means they are less likely to reproduce.


“These particles are found in the air in most cities. So, if the effect is the same for human beings as it is for rats, it could be that pollution is having a significant impact on human fertility.”

Dr. Andrew Shennan, also of the University of Edinburgh’s School of Biological Sciences, added: “In many industrialized cities around the world, infertility is more common than we realized. Our study suggests that part of the reason for this could be due to air pollution.”

Professor Charles said the next step would be to test whether human cells react in the same way when exposed to pollution particles.

Source: University of Edinburgh

“We can’t say for sure that the changes we see in the levels of sex hormones and in anatomy are due to vanadium,” said lead researcher Dr. Rodrigo Morales of the National Autonomous University of Mexico. “But what we can say is that there is a correlation or connection between the changes we see and the vanadium treatment.”

Previous research has suggested a link between vanadium and reproductive health. But the new study is among the first to look at the effects of vanadium on the anatomy of the reproductive system and the levels of sex hormones, according to Morales.

To see how vanadium affects reproductive health, the researchers gave groups of rats different doses of vanadium, once a day for 60 days. They then examined the rats’ ventral prostate — an anatomical structure specific to male rodents that’s difficult to find in other animals, Morales said.

They also looked at the ischiocavernosus and bulbourethral muscles, which are important for male urination. In healthy males, these muscles contract to help eject urine from the body.

In addition, the researchers took tissue samples from the rats’ seminal vesicles — an organ that is part of the male reproductive system and helps produce ejaculatory fluid.

Finally, the researchers measured levels of sex hormones in the blood of the male rats.

The researchers found that low doses of vanadium had no effect on the rats’ anatomy or levels of sex hormones. But levels of two hormones — testosterone and luteinizing hormone — were decreased by about 50% with medium doses, and by about 70% with high doses of vanadium.

Testicular tissue from the rats that were given high-dose vanadium showed a decrease in the number of egg-producing cells, Morales said.

The changes to the rats’ reproductive system were specific to the type of vanadium compound the rats received, the researchers found. Rats given one compound had changes to their semen, for example, while rats given a different compound had changes to their reproductive tract anatomy.

The researchers also found that, in general, higher doses of vanadium led to greater changes to the rats’ reproductive systems. Changes in urine-ejecting muscles were among the most obvious effects of all the vanadium doses, the researchers reported.

The findings add to earlier evidence that vanadium may pose a risk to reproductive health, the researchers said.

Previous research has suggested that vanadium causes DNA damage that could lead to mutations and is toxic to cells in the reproductive system, the researchers said.

The researchers studied the effects of pollution on the blood parameters of four animal species: two fish (catfish Clarias gariepinus and tilapia Oreochromis niloticus), and two birds (the moorhen Gallinula chloropus and the maskew’s francolin Pternistis loveri). They found that the animals living in more polluted water had changes in their blood biochemistry, which showed up as changes in the levels of certain proteins, or biomarkers, in their blood. For example, the levels of protein enzymes in the blood can indicate whether an animal has organ damage or immune system stress.
The researchers also found that the type of pollution affected the different species differently. For example, the effects of industrial waste were more pronounced in the fish than in the birds, while the effects of domestic waste were more pronounced in the birds than in the fish.
Dr Magda Abd El-Aal, one of the researchers on the study, said “Animals living in polluted environments may not show any obvious signs of stress, so it’s not always possible to tell how pollution is affecting them just by looking at them. However, changes in blood chemistry can tell us a lot about the health of individual animals, and how their bodies are responding to their environment.”
Dr Abd El-Aal works at the National Research Centre in Egypt, where she is a principal researcher and expert in fish pathology. She collaborated on this study with Dr Moattam Aldaff, a fish pathologist at the same institution, and with Drs Magdi El-Samrani and Ahmed Mansour, a fish biologist and a zoologist respectively, also from the National Research Centre.
Dr El-Samrani, who is the first author of the paper, said “In future, we would like to carry out longer studies, over several months, to see how the effects of pollution change over time. We would also like to study the effects of pollution on other animals, including mammals.”
Dr Aldaff added “Pollution is a serious problem, not just in Egypt but worldwide, and it is important that we understand how it is affecting the animals that live in polluted environments, and how this may be affecting the food chain and, potentially, human health.”
Dr El-Samrani and Dr Mansour are both based at the Department of Animal and Fish Resources Laboratory, National Research Centre.

samples.ref: Enkozesa y’Obuwangwa ey’Ebimera by’omu Mpya mu Kitundu ky’omu North West Ethiopia
samples.hyp:
The study aimed to investigate the use of homegarden plants in an indigenous community in North West Ethiopia. An ethnobotanical survey was conducted in five villages of the Dembla and Tele communities in North West Ethiopia between June and November 2014. Data were collected using semi-structured in-depth interviews, key-informant interviews, field observations, and a voucher specimen. Ethnomedicinal data were analyzed using the Feyera index, while ethnobotanical data were analyzed using the culture element methodology. A total of 97 use-taxa were reported, belonging to 51 genera and 24 families. The most frequently mentioned families were Poaceae, Lamiaceae, Rubiaceae, Fabaceae, and Verbenaceae. The most frequently mentioned use-categories were food, fodder, medicine, fuelwood, and construction. The most frequently mentioned plants were four fodder plants: Cenchrus ciliaris, Eleusine coracana, Panicum maximum, and Senecio giganthemum. The most frequently mentioned plants in the food use-category were Cenchrus ciliaris, Eleusine coracana, and Senecio giganthemum. The Feyera index revealed that the most popular plants for ethnomedicinal purposes were Cenchrus ciliaris, Eleusine coracana, and Senecio giganthemum. The study also investigated the effect of management intensity on the structure of homegardens and their surrounding forests. The results showed that homegardens in the Tele community were more intensively managed than those in the Dembla community. The structure of homegardens in the Tele community was characterized by a high tree density, a young stand dominated by shrubs and herbs, a high species diversity, and a high tree basal area. The homegardens in the Dembla community had a low tree density, an older stand dominated by trees, a low species diversity, and a low tree basal area. The study concluded that the homegarden is an important cultural landscape in the indigenous communities in North West Ethiopia. The homegarden is a product of cultural evolution and a human response to adapt to upland conditions. The study also concluded that the homegarden is a dynamic system that combines agricultural and forest resources, and that the intensity of garden management can affect the structure of homegardens and their surrounding forests.

samples.hyp: Homegardens, which are vital to the well-being of many in the developing world, are a largely untapped resource for the conservation of plant diversity and maintenance of local food production systems. This research is conducted in the Sierra de los Altos region of Veracruz, Mexico. Homegardens are a important cultural practice in the region, where they have been used for at least 500 years. The information gathered from this research will be used to inform local conservation and reforestation efforts, and to create a model for other regions that have similar cultural practices. This research will be conducted over the course of four field seasons. During the first, floristic inventory data was collected and botanical specimens were gathered. During the second, ethnobotanical data was collected through semi-structured interviews. From these data sets, the cultural importance of plant species in homegardens will be assessed. During the third field season, the results of the floristic and ethnobotanical surveys will be presented back to community members. The results of this research will be used to create a public display and a management plan for homegarden conservation in the region. During the final field season, the public presentation and management plan will be implemented. This research is significant because it will provide a framework for the conservation of homegardens, and a model for the preservation of plant diversity in ethnobotanical landscapes. The research will focus on the Floristic and Ethnobotanical Composition of Homegarden Landscapes in the Sierra de Los Altos, Veracruz, Mexico. Specific objectives include 1) inventorying the plant species in homegardens and assessing the levels of threat to the species; 2) documenting the uses of plants in homegardens; 3) determining the cultural importance of plants in homegardens; 4) using vegetation modeling to assess the composition of homegardens; 5) presenting research results to community members; 6) using focus groups to assess community perceptions of selected plant species; and 7) developing a management plan for homegarden conservation. Xela, wa xelarab, xela xelarab.  (CASH 2019) 

Xela is the name of a plant. 

Xela is a vine that is used for making hammocks. The fibers are used to weave the hammocks. 

The plant is called xela because its fruit resembles the face of an old woman. 

The fruit is green and is a pod that contains several seeds. 

The plant is found in the mountains. 

This plant can be eaten. 

The plant is not used for medicinal purposes. 

Key to Symbolism 

Xela (Bignonia capreolata) is a native vine of the tropical Americas. It is commonly known by a number of other names including climbing trumpet vine, cow’s head vine, yellow trumpet, yellow gentian, golden trumpet, and jungle jazz (Standard 2002). The plant has become an invasive species in many parts of the world including Australia, South Africa, and Hawaii (Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council 2010). 

The common name of the plant, cow’s head vine, alludes to the shape of the leaf and the color of the flower. The leaf is reniform and the flower is red and yellow. 

The specific epithet capreolata derives from the Latin capreolus, “chamois” or “ibex,” and means “goat-like” (Standard 2002). The shape of the leaf resembles a goat’s head. 

The generic name Bignonia honors Charles Plumier, who was a French botanist, missionary, and artist. Plumier was also a physician to the wealthy in the French Caribbean, and an amateur naturalist. He collected many plant and animal specimens in the West Indies and sent them to the Linnean Society in Europe (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew 2018). 

The species name was first published in the journal Systema Naturae in 1759 by the German zoologist and botanist, Carl Linna

This study aims to evaluate the role of tribal groups in food security and biodiversity conservation in the Western Ghats of India, a biodiversity hotspot. Semi-structured questionnaires were used to interview 120 tribal individuals from three different locations. The significance of the association of different variables with food security was evaluated using a Poisson regression model. In the study area, 84.17% of the tribal population reside below the poverty line. More than 90% of the population depend on agriculture for their livelihood, and food security is more likely in tribal groups with higher forest dependence. The food security of tribal groups is at a higher risk of being affected by the out-migration of the population. Our study suggests that the forest-based economy is a key factor to maintain both food security and biodiversity. Thus, we need to focus on the reviving of forest-based economies among the tribal groups to ensure their livelihood and to conserve biodiversity.

Tribal people, also known as indigenous people, are the original inhabitants of a given region or country who have a distinct culture, language, and beliefs (Anon. 2019). They are often isolated, marginilized, and considered to be vulnerable (Nilsson, 2003). The tribal population in India is estimated to be around 65 million (Anon., 2019) and they constitute about 8.6% of the total population in the country (Anon., 2019). Abstract and Keywords

Ethiopia is one of the countries hit hard by the COVID-19 pandemic. To minimize person-to-person transmission of the virus, the Ethiopian government declared a state of emergency and other restrictive measures. These measures have many adverse socioeconomic impacts on communities. Gardens and trees around urban and peri-urban areas can contribute to food security and conservation in multiple ways. This article provides a summary of the various ways in which domestic and community gardens as well as street trees in Ethiopian cities contribute to food security of communities and conservation of the environment and natural resources. It ends with a discussion about the potential of urban forestry and gardening in the context of the current pandemic and beyond.

The team used machine learning to identify patterns in the language used in the tweets. The algorithm was trained on a set of 10,000 tweets in English, French, and Spanish that were either racist or not. It accurately identified racist content in 80% of instances in English, 60% in French, and 70% in Spanish.
